title: From Qubit Tensorization To Gaussian Optimizers In Bosonic Systems
authors: Hami Mehrabi Salman Beigi
abstract: ArXiv:2610.28902v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a method for deriving Gaussian optimality results for bosonic quantum systems from inequalities for qubit systems. Inspired by Gross's derivation of the Gaussian logarithmic Sobolev inequality from an inequality on the two-point space, we use qubits as quantum two-point spaces and lift bosonic Weyl operators to pseudo-Weyl operators on large qubit systems. By controlling weighted norms and relative entropy in the fluctuation limit, we establish two transfer theorems that convert tensorized qubit inequalities into inequalities for bosonic Gaussian channels. As a first application, we prove that the sharp [MATH]-logarithmic Sobolev inequality for the bosonic Ornstein--Uhlenbeck semigroup tensorizes without loss in the constant. We also establish a sharp output entropy inequality for tensor powers of a class of qubit channels. This includes a quantum Mrs.~Gerber's lemma determining the minimum output entropy of tensor powers of the qubit depolarizing channel at fixed input entropy. Applying our relative entropy transfer theorem, we obtain multimode constrained minimum output entropy bounds for Gaussian additive-noise channels and thermal attenuators in the heating range.
tldr: The paper develops a qubit-to-boson transfer method that derives Gaussian optimality and entropy inequalities for bosonic quantum systems from tensorized qubit inequalities.
motivation: Gaussian optimizers are central to quantum information with continuous-variable systems, but proving sharp Gaussian optimality results can be technically difficult; the authors aim to import powerful qubit inequalities into the bosonic setting.
method: They lift bosonic Weyl operators to pseudo-Weyl operators on large qubit systems and prove transfer theorems controlling weighted norms and relative entropy in a fluctuation limit, converting tensorized qubit inequalities into Gaussian channel inequalities.
result: They show that the sharp logarithmic Sobolev inequality for the bosonic Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup tensorizes without loss, prove sharp output entropy inequalities for tensor powers of certain qubit channels including a quantum Mrs. Gerber's lemma for the depolarizing channel, and derive multimode constrained minimum output entropy bounds for Gaussian additive-noise channels and thermal attenuators.
conclusion: The work provides a general route from qubit tensorization to Gaussian optimizer theorems and yields sharp continuous-variable entropy inequalities with applications to Gaussian channels.

title: Bias-Preserving Entanglement Of Kerr-Cat Qubits With An Ats Coupler
authors: Kerem Yurtseven, Shantanu R. Jha, Apoorva Limaye, Risav Pokhrel, Muhammad Waqar Amin
abstract: ArXiv:2610.28749v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Kerr-cat qubits offer a hardware-efficient route to fault-tolerant quantum computing by suppressing bit-flip errors exponentially, while phase-flip errors increase only linearly with the mean photon number. To maintain this protection, entangling operations must be bias-preserving, ensuring that phase-flip errors occurring during the gate do not propagate into bit-flip errors. In this paper, we propose an asymmetrically threaded SQUID (ATS) parametric coupler to implement high-fidelity, bias-preserving entangling gates between Kerr-cat qubits. By engineering a photon-number asymmetry between the control and target modes, we enable fast gate operations that suppress non-adiabatic leakage without complex pulse shaping. Through numerical simulations of the full circuit Hamiltonian, we demonstrate a bias-preserving CX gate achieving 99.69% fidelity in the absence of photon loss for a gate duration of 50 ns. Under a single-photon loss rate of 100 kHz, our protocol yields a noise bias of 9922, exceeding the noise bias of a naive non-bias-preserving CX implementation by approximately a factor of 570. These results support the ATS coupler as a valuable building block for concatenated cat-qubit architectures.

result: They demonstrate a bias-preserving CX gate with 99.69% fidelity in the absence of photon loss for a 50 ns gate, and under 100 kHz single-photon loss they obtain a noise bias of 9922, about 570 times larger than a naive non-bias-preserving CX.
conclusion: The ATS coupler is a promising building block for concatenated cat-qubit architectures and fault-tolerant superconducting quantum computing.

title: Algebraic Criteria For Complete Relaxation In Autonomous And Periodically Driven Open Quantum Systems
authors: Kay Brandner Paul Menczel
abstract: ArXiv:2610.29084v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We derive sufficient criteria that guarantee convergence of open quantum system dynamics to a unique long-time state independent of the initial conditions. We refer to this behavior as complete relaxation. Focusing on systems described by Gorini-Kossakowski-Sudarshan-Lindblad (GKSL) master equations on finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces, our approach uses only elementary mathematical arguments. For autonomous systems, we recover three previously derived relaxation criteria, which can be expressed as algebraic conditions on the Lindblad operators and the Hamiltonian entering the GKSL equation. For periodically driven systems, we obtain a new criterion involving a similar algebraic condition and a local continuity requirement on the time-dependent GKSL generator. This result implies an earlier criterion for complete relaxation formulated in Ref. [J. Phys. A 52, 43LT01 (2019)]. We also discuss implications of our approach for periodically modulated classical master equations, as well as extensions to driven systems without a periodicity constraint.
tldr: The paper derives algebraic sufficient criteria for complete relaxation, i.e., convergence to a unique initial-state-independent long-time state, in autonomous and periodically driven GKSL open quantum systems.
motivation: Relaxation to a unique steady state is a fundamental property of open quantum dynamics, but general and mathematically simple criteria are useful for both autonomous and driven Lindblad systems.
method: Using elementary mathematical arguments, the authors formulate algebraic conditions on Lindblad operators and the Hamiltonian for autonomous GKSL equations, and extend them to periodically driven systems via an additional local continuity condition on the time-dependent generator.
result: The approach recovers three known autonomous relaxation criteria and yields a new criterion for periodically driven systems that implies an earlier result, with extensions to periodically modulated classical master equations and non-periodic driving.
conclusion: The derived algebraic criteria provide practical sufficient conditions for complete relaxation in open quantum systems and clarify connections among existing relaxation results.

title: Convergence Analysis Of The Quantum Blahut-Arimoto Algorithm And The Contraction Coefficient Of Qubit Amplitude-Damping Channels
authors: Yonglong Li Junke Han
abstract: ArXiv:2610.29373v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this work, we investigate the convergence rate of the quantum Blahut-Arimoto (BA) algorithm proposed for computing the coherent information of less noisy quantum channels. Previous work established exponential convergence under certain restrictive assumptions on the channel. Using a Taylor expansion around a positive definite optimizer, we show that, for an injective degradable channel whose degrading channel has a relative-entropy contraction coefficient strictly less than one, the algorithm converges at an exponential rate after sufficiently many iterations. We further verify this condition for qubit amplitude-damping (AD) channels in the relevant parameter regime. In addition, by analyzing the Bogoliubov-Kubo-Mori (BKM) metric on the Bloch ball, we derive an explicit characterization of the relative-entropy contraction coefficient of qubit AD channels. The proposed approach is further extended to calculate the relative contraction coefficient and the relative expansion coefficient of two qubit AD channels.

title: Quantum Belief Characterization: A Multi-Shot Notion Of Equivalence
authors: Mingxuan Liu, Pavel Sekatski, Valerio Scarani
abstract: ArXiv:2610.29450v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A recent formulation of quantum belief showed that quantum retrodiction depends not only on the reduced density operator of the system of interest, but also on correlations with a hidden reference system, which leads to the notion of quantum belief equivalence. In this paper we formulate a multi-shot problem, where the extended posterior obtained after one update is used again as the prior for the next update. We first define a formal notion of [MATH]-shot equivalence and derive several propositions for arbitrary extended beliefs. We then argue that the agent must also specify why the data obtained in different rounds concern the same underlying object. Through the quantum de Finetti representation, this narrows the one-copy belief to a special class: candidate-state ensemble belief. In that sector, we show that two beliefs are [MATH]-shot equivalent if and only if their [MATH]-th moments are equal. abstract: ArXiv:2610.28748v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computers need fast and accurate error decoding. title: Low-field Dephasing Time Of An Optically Polarized Nv$^-$ Spin Bath Beyond The P1 Limit In Diamond: A Cluster-correlation-expansion And Exact Spin-bath Study

abstract: ArXiv:2610.28737v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Calderbank--Shor--Steane (CSS) codes support decoding and fault-tolerant logical operations through separate pure [MATH] and pure [MATH] stabilizer checks. The lower bound uses interpolation to construct positive mean-one priors and controls their distinguishability and entropy separation after normalization. Exact count-variance identities and weighted approximation duality connect the two arguments.
tldr: The paper characterizes minimax sample complexity for estimating classical Rényi entropy and logarithmic additive functional entropy from independent samples.
motivation: Entropy estimation is a fundamental statistical problem, and sharp minimax rates are sought for Rényi entropies across varying orders and alphabet sizes.
method: The authors prove matching upper and lower bounds using polynomial approximation, Gamma count statistics, an independent pilot, interpolation priors, and weighted approximation duality.
result: They obtain tight sample-complexity rates for Rényi entropy estimation, including uniform behavior near integer and order-one limits, and extend the analysis to logarithms of positive additive functionals.
conclusion: The work provides a complete minimax characterization for classical Rényi and logarithmic additive functional entropy estimation, showing regularity alone does not determine complexity.

title: A Matroidal Framework For Random Access In Linear Codes
authors: Daniella Bar-Lev, Hiram H. L\'opez, Gretchen L. Matthews, Flavio Salizzoni
abstract: ArXiv:2610.28820v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study random access in linear codes when codeword symbols are sampled independently and uniformly with replacement. A code is recovery balanced if the expected number of samples required to recover a codeword coordinate is the same for every coordinate. We express the recovery expectations in terms of the associated matroid and derive a coordinatewise identity relating these values for a code and its dual. This proves that a linear code is recovery balanced if and only if its dual is recovery balanced, establishing a conjecture of Gruica et al. We further define the recovery balance for arbitrary matroids and show that asymptotically almost every sparse paving matroid is not recovery balanced.
tldr: The paper introduces recovery-balanced linear codes, expresses random-access recovery expectations via matroids, and proves that a code is recovery balanced if and only if its dual is.
motivation: Random access recovery may require different expected sample counts depending on the codeword coordinate, motivating a structural characterization of when these expectations are uniform across coordinates.
method: The authors formulate recovery expectations in terms of the matroid associated with a linear code, derive a coordinatewise identity connecting a code and its dual, and extend recovery balance to arbitrary matroids.
result: They prove the conjecture of Gruica et al. that recovery balance is dual-symmetric for linear codes, and show that asymptotically almost every sparse paving matroid is not recovery balanced.
conclusion: The matroidal framework provides a clean structural explanation of random-access recovery balance and its dual invariance, though the work is classical coding theory without direct quantum information implications.

title: Fast Template Matching For Quantum Circuits Using Hypergraph
authors: Xin Hong, Jintao Yu, Runhong He, Shenggang Ying, Sanjiang Li, Mingsheng Ying
abstract: ArXiv:2610.29095v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum circuit optimization is a key step toward the efficient execution of quantum algorithms. Template matching has emerged as one of the dominant approaches for simplifying quantum circuits, yet it confronts the intrinsic challenge of accommodating gate commutativity. The state-of-the-art template-matching algorithm relies on a directed acyclic graph (DAG) representation. While this DAG-based technique handles gate commutativity satisfactorily, it fails to preserve the local connectivity inherent to quantum circuits, thereby leading to relatively high matching complexity. In this paper, we introduce a hypergraph representation (HG), a commutativity-aware representation that collapses commuting gates into a single super-node while retaining all local connectivity. This enables matches to be extended locally without revisiting the rest of the circuit, with incremental updates limited to the immediate neighborhood. Experimental results demonstrate that our HG matcher achieves 11--606x speed-up over the DAG-based implementation in Qiskit (Iten et al., 2022) on both random and arithmetic benchmarks, while maintaining the same optimization quality. The acceleration increases with circuit size, confirming that preserving locality and connectivity is the key to scalable quantum circuit optimisation.
tldr: Introduces a hypergraph representation for quantum circuit template matching that collapses commuting gates into super-nodes to preserve locality and yield 11–606x speedups over the DAG-based Qiskit matcher.
motivation: Template matching is a dominant circuit simplification technique, but the standard DAG representation destroys local connectivity, making matching complex and poorly scalable as circuits grow.
method: The authors propose a commutativity-aware hypergraph representation in which mutually commuting gates are merged into a single super-node, allowing matches to be extended locally with incremental updates restricted to the immediate neighborhood.
result: On random and arithmetic benchmarks the hypergraph matcher achieves 11–606x speed-up over the Qiskit DAG-based implementation while maintaining identical optimization quality, with acceleration growing with circuit size.
conclusion: Preserving locality and connectivity is the key to scalable quantum circuit optimization; the hypergraph approach offers a substantially faster, quality-neutral alternative to DAG-based template matching.

title: Stochastic Resonance In Time-delayed Bistable Active Particles
authors: Antonio A. Valido, Mattia Coccolo, Miguel A. F. Sanju\'an
abstract: ArXiv:2610.29601v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate analytically and numerically stochastic resonance in an underdamped active (Ornstein--Uhlenbeck) particle confined in a bistable potential with time-delayed feedback and subjected to an additional (non-thermal) white-noise source. Restricting the analysis to the active-noise-dominated bistable regime, with sufficiently short delay and active-noise correlation times, we develop a perturbative theory that yields analytical expressions for both the escape rate and the spectral power amplification within the framework of linear-response theory, without invoking detailed balance. The analytical predictions are in qualitative agreement with direct numerical simulations throughout the perturbative regime. We show that a moderate increase in the active-noise correlation time can enhance the stochastic-resonance response, in marked contrast to previous results for overdamped passive systems driven by colored noise. Conversely, the addition of white noise weakens the resonant response and shifts its optimum toward lower active-noise intensities. Time-delayed feedback further alters the matching condition between the escape rate and the driving frequency while preserving the resonant mechanism. Beyond the perturbative regime, we find that finite-memory effects progressively broaden the resonance profile and substantially decrease its amplitude. Overall, these results provide new insight into the combined role of inertia, activity, environmental fluctuations, and time delayed feedback in stochastic resonance in nonequilibrium systems.
tldr: An analytical and numerical study of stochastic resonance in an underdamped active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck particle in a bistable potential with time-delayed feedback and extra white noise.
motivation: Stochastic resonance is well studied in passive overdamped systems, but how inertia, active (colored) noise, and delayed feedback jointly shape resonant response in nonequilibrium active matter is not understood.
method: Perturbative linear-response theory (without detailed balance) yields analytic expressions for the escape rate and spectral power amplification in the active-noise-dominated regime, validated against direct numerical simulations.
result: Moderate increases in active-noise correlation time enhance the stochastic-resonance response (opposite to overdamped passive colored-noise results), added white noise weakens and shifts the resonance, and delay alters the escape-rate/driving-frequency matching while finite memory broadens and suppresses the resonance profile.
conclusion: The work clarifies the combined roles of inertia, activity, environmental noise, and time-delayed feedback in stochastic resonance, offering guidance for controlling noise-induced response in nonequilibrium classical systems.

title: On Almost Mds Codes Holding $(n-k-1)$-designs And An Open Problem On Witt Design
authors: Huakai Wei, Shiyuan Qiang, Shaofang Hong
abstract: ArXiv:2610.29744v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let [MATH] be an almost maximum distance separable (AMDS) code over the finite fields with parameters [MATH] whose minimum-weight codewords support an [MATH]-[MATH] design. We first determine the parameters of the dual code [MATH]. We also characterize the design and its complementary design supported by the minimum weight codewords of [MATH]. In particular, we present explicit formulas for the weight enumerators of all subset codes of [MATH] with length at least [MATH]. These formulas are completely determined by the cardinality of the subset, the dimension, together with the parameter [MATH], and are independent of the specific choice of subsets. motivation: The work is motivated by classical coding theory and combinatorial design theory, specifically characterizing designs supported by minimum-weight codewords and answering a 2023 open problem.
method: The authors determine parameters of the dual code, characterize the supported design and its complementary design, and derive explicit weight enumerators for subset codes of length at least a certain threshold.

conclusion: The paper advances classical coding theory and combinatorial designs but has no direct connection to quantum information, quantum thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Higher-Order Flatband-Touching Points Mediate Unconventional Bulk-Boundary Correspondence
authors: Limin Song, Jianqi Xiong, Liqin Tang, Daohong Song, Zhigang Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2610.29251v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The bulk-boundary correspondence establishes a fundamental connection between bulk band topology and the emergence of boundary states, underpinning topological phenomena across electronic, acoustic, photonic, and many other wave systems. A broad class of singular flatband systems, however, exhibits an unconventional form of bulk-boundary correspondence, in which robust boundary modes (RBMs) originate from flatband-touching points (FBTPs) and the real-space topology associated with incomplete sets of compact localized states (CLSs), rather than conventional momentum-space bulk topological invariants. To date, experimental studies of such boundary modes have been limited to systems hosting lower-order FBTPs. Here, we experimentally demonstrate unconventional bulk-boundary correspondence in a photonic cross-bedded Kagome-like lattice featuring a higher-order FBTP formed by the touching of two degenerate flatbands and a dispersive band. Using continuous-wave laser writing, we observe shape-preserving propagation of both bulk CLSs and boundary RBMs. Remarkably, unlike previously reported flatband systems, the RBMs retain their boundary localization under input-field perturbations involving both singular and nonsingular CLSs, revealing an unconventional boundary response associated with the higher-order FBTP in this lattice. Our results establish the Kagome-like lattice as a new platform for exploring flatband physics and unconventional bulk-boundary correspondence, with potential applications in wave localization, flatband lasers, and other emerging topological photonic devices.
tldr: The authors experimentally demonstrate an unconventional bulk-boundary correspondence in a photonic cross-bedded Kagome-like lattice, where robust boundary modes arise from a higher-order flatband-touching point formed by two degenerate flatbands and one dispersive band.
motivation: Flatband systems with singular band-touching points show boundary modes that cannot be explained by conventional momentum-space topological invariants, but experiments have so far been limited to lower-order flatband-touching points.
method: Continuous-wave laser writing is used to fabricate a photonic Kagome-like lattice, and propagation of compact localized states and boundary modes is observed under continuous-wave excitation, including perturbations of the input field.
result: Both bulk compact localized states and boundary robust boundary modes propagate in a shape-preserving way, and the boundary modes remain localized even under perturbations mixing singular and nonsingular compact localized states.
conclusion: The Kagome-like lattice provides a platform for flatband physics and higher-order flatband-touching-mediated boundary modes, with potential uses in wave localization and topological photonic devices.

title: Support Periods Of Polynomials And Support-primitive Decomposition Of Constacyclic Codes Over Galois Rings
authors: Hongfeng Wu Li Zhu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.29284v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let \(A=\GR(p^e,r)\) have residue field \(\F_q\), and let \(\lambda\in A^\times\). We relate coefficient compression of monic divisors of \(X^N-\lambda\) to support-primitive decomposition of constacyclic codes. At a simple-root length, the support period of every nonconstant monic divisor is preserved at each coefficient precision and equals the order of the multiplicative stabilizer of its root set. For a cyclic Frobenius-orbit polynomial, the multiple equal-difference structure determines its support period, core degree, and least relative degree of an unramified extension over which all its basic-irreducible factors are binomials. Coordinate projections give every constacyclic code over a finite commutative ring a unique maximal interleaving into copies of one support-primitive code. At simple-root lengths over \(A\), the intrinsic period of a code is the greatest common divisor of the periods of its torsion codes. The decomposition yields distance and duality formulas and the arithmetic Singleton bound for free codes. At every length, a nonzero code over \(A\) has the same minimum Hamming distance as its highest torsion code, which gives a refined bound. At repeated-root lengths, identical torsion filtrations can occur with different intrinsic periods, while a class of nonzero codes obtained by substitution from simple-root generators retains the same core and minimum distance. Trace matrices recover the coefficients of basic-irreducible cores using unit pivots, and local Hensel corrections lift compressed factors directly. For \(X^n-1\) with \(p\nmid n\), lifting and output have quasi-linear bit cost in the compressed representation when the arithmetic data and residue factorizations are given.
tldr: The paper studies support periods of polynomials and support-primitive decomposition of constacyclic codes over Galois rings, with applications to distance and duality bounds.
motivation: The work aims to understand structural decompositions of constacyclic codes over finite commutative rings, extending algebraic coding-theoretic results on polynomial divisors and torsion codes.
method: It relates coefficient compression of monic divisors of X^N - lambda to support-primitive decompositions, analyzes support periods via root-set stabilizers, and uses torsion filtrations, trace matrices, and Hensel corrections.
result: The authors obtain unique maximal interleavings, distance and duality formulas, arithmetic Singleton bounds, and refined minimum-distance bounds via highest torsion codes, including quasi-linear complexity for lifting in simple-root cases.
conclusion: The paper advances classical algebraic coding theory over Galois rings but has no direct connection to quantum information, quantum thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Can Quantum Layers Offer Performance And Security Advantages In Vision-Language Models?
authors: Alvi Ataur Khalil Md Khalid Syfullah
abstract: ArXiv:2610.28964v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As quantum computing moves from the noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) era toward early fault-tolerant quantum computing (EFTQC), quantum-enhanced AI is shifting from a conceptual idea to experimental research. Quantum components are expected to extend the capabilities of existing AI systems, yet it remains unclear how such components will help within large multimodal models. In this study, we try to answer that question for vision-language models (VLMs) using classically simulated quantum layers. With LLaVA-OneVision as the backbone, we evaluate 4- and 8-qubit basic-ring and strongly entangling circuits at four insertion and four replacement locations. Insertion adds quantum layers to the classical model, while replacement substitutes them for classical components. Using the same setup, we compare performance and computational cost between classical and quantum-classical hybrid models. On the Visual Spatial Reasoning dataset, inserting a quantum layer after the visual projector reaches 80.7% development accuracy, 2.28 percentage-points above classical full fine-tuning. Replacing the final decoder feed-forward sublayer retains 79.22% accuracy with 13.07 million fewer trainable parameters. Quantum insertion can thus improve accuracy, and selective replacement can reduce parameters. These benefits depend strongly on where the quantum layer is inserted or which classical component it replaces: earlier replacements lower accuracy, and fewer parameters do not reliably shorten training or reduce computation. To assess potential security benefits, we evaluated the robustness of quantum-classical hybrid models under six attack settings. Overall, our study maps where quantum layers help and hurt within VLMs, offering a starting point for hybrid VLM design; whether these gains generalize remains open. The code is available at [URL].
tldr: An empirical study inserting or replacing classically simulated quantum layers (4- and 8-qubit ring and strongly entangling circuits) in the LLaVA-OneVision vision-language model to measure accuracy, parameter count, and adversarial robustness.
motivation: Quantum-enhanced AI is transitioning from concept to experiment, but it is unclear whether quantum components actually help inside large multimodal models, and where they should be placed.
method: Using classically simulated variational quantum circuits at four insertion and four replacement locations in a LLaVA-OneVision backbone, the authors compare classical and hybrid models on the Visual Spatial Reasoning dataset in accuracy, trainable parameters, and computational cost, and evaluate robustness under six attack settings.
result: Inserting a quantum layer after the visual projector yields 80.7% dev accuracy (2.28 points above classical full fine-tuning), while replacing the final decoder feed-forward sublayer retains 79.22% accuracy with 13.07M fewer trainable parameters; earlier replacements degrade accuracy and parameter savings do not reliably reduce training time.
conclusion: Quantum layers may offer modest accuracy or parameter-efficiency benefits in VLMs depending sensitively on placement, but the work is an exploratory applied mapping rather than an information-theoretic or thermodynamic result, and generalization remains open.

title: From Common Information To Canonical Correlation Analysis And Beyond: Bridging Information Theory, Signal Processing, And Machine Learning
authors: Walid Saad Paris A. Karakasis
abstract: ArXiv:2610.28978v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many problems in signal processing, machine learning, and neuroimaging provide several jointly observed measurements of one process, each mixing a component common to all of them with a component private to itself, and require the common component to be recovered without supervision. This problem has been studied in several communities, largely independently. Statisticians proposed canonical correlation analysis (CCA), introduced by Hotelling in 1936. Information theorists proposed two notions of common information, due to G\'acs and K\"orner and to Wyner. Engineers developed subspace methods for sensor arrays and multiuser communications to design multiview receivers. This tutorial presents the main results and tools each community developed for this problem in a single exposition, and explains the connections that emerge where they meet, distinguishing exact equivalences from special cases and analogies. We develop the information-theoretic foundation from first principles. We then introduce CCA and its extension to several views, followed by the engineering thread from blind multiuser detection to CCA as a blind receiver. Next, we turn to nonlinear CCA, covering kernel, deep, and probabilistic formulations, the conditions under which the common factor is identifiable, and connections to self-supervised learning. We conclude with a discussion of further extensions and open directions. The exposition is self-contained, so that readers from each of these communities can follow the parts developed by the others.
tldr: A self-contained tutorial unifying two notions of common information (Gács–Körner and Wyner), canonical correlation analysis, blind multiuser detection, and nonlinear/kernel/deep CCA into a single exposition aimed at bridging information theory, signal processing, and machine learning.
motivation: The problem of recovering a component shared by several jointly observed, mixed measurements has been studied independently by statisticians, information theorists, and engineers, so the authors aim to consolidate these parallel literatures and clarify which connections are exact equivalences versus analogies or special cases.
method: Tutorial-style development: information-theoretic foundations of common information from first principles, then CCA and its multiview extension, subspace/blind-receiver engineering methods, and nonlinear CCA variants (kernel, deep, probabilistic) with identifiability conditions and links to self-supervised learning.
result: The paper organizes and cross-references existing results rather than proving new theorems, distinguishing precise equivalences (e.g., between CCA and blind multiuser detection as a blind receiver) from merely suggestive parallels, and cataloguing identifiability conditions for the common-factor model.
conclusion: The tutorial serves as a unified reference for common-information and CCA methods across communities and outlines open directions for further extensions, but contributes no quantum information-theoretic content.

title: Some Results On The Weight Spectrum Of Binary Reed-Muller Codes $RM(m-7,m)$

abstract: ArXiv:2610.29807v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the set of weights occurring in the high-order binary Reed-Muller codes [MATH]. The proof first establishes the corresponding base-code inclusion in [MATH]. result: For every m ≥ 14 the weight spectrum of RM(m-7,m) contains all even weights in an explicit interval together with a finite set of low weights and their complements, and several construction routes are shown to be incapable of producing the four remaining unresolved base-code weights.
conclusion: The work substantially sharpens the open spectrum problem for RM(m-7,m), narrowing the unresolved weights and delineating which concatenation-based constructions cannot succeed, while leaving four base-code weights open.

title: Pushing Beyond The Memory Barrier In Propagation Algorithms With Randomization
authors: Manuel S. Rudolph, Ricard Puig, Slimane Thabet, Zo\"{e} Holmes
abstract: ArXiv:2610.28845v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Performant classical tools for simulating quantum circuits are important for benchmarking and supporting upcoming quantum devices. Pauli propagation offers promising capabilities, but deep circuits usually cause a rapid growth in the number of Pauli strings and can quickly exhaust the available memory. In this work, we introduce a randomized protocol that combines a specialized resampling schedule, merging, and a controlled amount of bias to keep the propagating Pauli sum within any prescribed memory budget. Additional computational resources can then be spent on embarrassingly parallel repetitions that systematically improve the estimate. Building on the open-source library PauliPropagation.jl, we show that 1) increasing memory of each simulation reduces the error systematically more than outside averaging, 2) resampling just enough to apply the next gate delays variance accumulation and gives better error-per-time trade-offs than more aggressive resampling, and 3) a small, controlled bias is crucial in cutting down variance and pushing far beyond unbiased randomization. The resulting framework can reproduce deterministic calculations while requiring several orders of magnitude less memory.
tldr: The paper introduces a randomized resampling protocol for Pauli propagation that keeps classical quantum-circuit simulations within a prescribed memory budget while controlling bias and variance.
motivation: Classical simulation of quantum circuits is important for benchmarking quantum devices, but Pauli propagation suffers from rapid growth in the number of Pauli strings for deep circuits, exhausting memory.
method: The authors combine a specialized resampling schedule, Pauli-string merging, and a controlled amount of bias to constrain the propagating Pauli sum to any memory budget, with additional embarrassingly parallel repetitions to improve estimates.
result: Using PauliPropagation.jl, they show that increasing per-simulation memory improves accuracy more systematically than outside averaging, minimal resampling delays variance accumulation, and a small controlled bias substantially reduces variance.
conclusion: The framework can reproduce deterministic calculations with orders of magnitude less memory, pushing classical Pauli-propagation simulations beyond previous memory barriers.

title: Digital Quantum Simulation Of Dynamics In Interacting Fields
authors: Zhiyao Li
abstract: ArXiv:2610.28993v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Matter under extreme conditions behaves as a non-equilibrium, strongly-interacting quantum system. Such systems are in the non-perturbative regime of quantum chromodynamics (QCD), where their time evolution is classically intractable. Quantum computing offers a promising alternative, but present-day devices are limited in qubit count and circuit depth, so efficient formulations and algorithms are key to scaling toward experimentally relevant QCD simulations. A scalable framework is established for simulating energy loss and hadronization in 1+1-dimensional SU(2) lattice gauge theory, in which a heavy quark traverses a lattice of light quarks. Classical lattice QCD methods are translated into physics-informed circuits to prepare the interacting ground state. The evolution is run on IBM's quantum processor ibm_pittsburgh, where the charge distribution and energy loss are measured. A further study develops the quantum simulation of the fully gauge-fixed SU(2) Hamiltonian in a mixed basis, a formulation that is expected to remain efficient at all gauge couplings. Digitizing the continuous gauge fields with as few as three qubits per plaquette reproduces low-energy observables with [MATH] precision. Scaling to larger systems is limited by resource overhead, which motivates truncations that preserve the relevant observables. Sequency Hierarchy Truncation (SeqHT) exploits the hierarchy in basis-operator contributions. Demonstrated on the adiabatic preparation of the [MATH] ground state on ibm_sherbrooke, SeqHT reduces circuit depth by ~30%, suppressing hardware noise in the extracted observables. All simulations in this dissertation are validated on quantum hardware against classical benchmarks. These studies advance quantum simulations of real-time QCD dynamics.
tldr: This dissertation develops scalable digital quantum-simulation methods for real-time dynamics in 1+1D SU(2) lattice gauge theory and demonstrates them on IBM superconducting quantum processors.
motivation: Strongly interacting matter in non-perturbative QCD is classically intractable, motivating quantum simulation, but near-term hardware limits qubit count and circuit depth.
method: The work maps lattice QCD dynamics into physics-informed quantum circuits, prepares interacting ground states, implements gauge-fixed SU(2) Hamiltonians in a mixed basis, and introduces Sequency Hierarchy Truncation to reduce circuit depth.
result: Charge distribution and energy loss are measured on ibm_pittsburgh, low-energy observables are reproduced with three qubits per plaquette at high precision, and SeqHT reduces circuit depth by about 30% on ibm_sherbrooke.
conclusion: The results advance hardware-validated quantum simulation of real-time QCD dynamics, though resource overhead remains a key scaling challenge.

title: Boundary Exceptional Point Driven Chiral Switch Of Topological Edge States
authors: Barsa Rani Sahu Bikashkali Midya
abstract: ArXiv:2610.29316v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We theoretically investigate the interplay of topology and localized non-Hermiticity in a finite Su-Schrieffer-Heeger chain characterized by non-Hermitian potentials at its boundaries. By tuning the boundary gain and loss parameters, we exploit the finite-size hybridization of two mid-gap topological edge states to analytically derive the exact coordinates of boundary-induced exceptional points (EPs), [MATH], at which these states undergo coalescence. We demonstrate that dynamically encircling these boundary EPs facilitates a robust, chiral edge state-transfer protocol. Depending on the orientation of the encircling loop, this protocol allows a topological edge state localized at one boundary to be either transferred to the opposite edge with perfect fidelity or returned to its starting position through a double switching process. Importantly, since the non-Hermiticity remains strictly confined to the boundaries, this chiral transport occurs without affecting the energy spectrum of the bulk bands. These results establish a minimal framework for a large-scale topological chiral switch that is experimentally verifiable and capable of being controlled through boundary non-Hermitian driving.
tldr: The paper theoretically studies boundary-induced exceptional points in a finite non-Hermitian Su-Schrieffer-Heeger chain and uses them for chiral topological edge-state transfer.
motivation: The authors aim to understand how localized non-Hermiticity at the boundaries of a finite topological chain affects hybridized mid-gap edge states and whether exceptional points can enable controlled state transfer.
method: They analytically derive the exceptional-point coordinates arising from finite-size hybridization of two topological edge states in an SSH chain with boundary gain and loss, and analyze dynamical encircling protocols around these points.
result: Encircling the boundary exceptional points produces a chiral switch: depending on the loop orientation, an edge state is either transferred to the opposite boundary with perfect fidelity or returned to its original position via a double-switching process, while the bulk spectrum remains unaffected.
conclusion: The work establishes a minimal, experimentally verifiable framework for boundary-controlled topological chiral switching, though it is not directly connected to the researcher's quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid-systems interests.

This improves the length [MATH] of Zeilberger, O'Connor, Gur and Spooner (2026), who observed that Dinur's gap amplification preserves zero knowledge. The simulator runs in expected polynomial time (or in strict polynomial time, with a failure symbol or with negligible statistical error). For [MATH] the length is [MATH], the form of the shortest known constant-query PCPs without zero knowledge. Unless NP [MATH] BPP, the dependence on [MATH] is optimal up to the polylogarithmic factor for polynomial-time simulators: zero knowledge is free up to linear query bounds. Zero-knowledge interactive oracle proofs achieved length [MATH] in 2016-17; we obtain it for PCPs. Gur, O'Connor and Spooner (STOC 2025) asked whether NP has such PCPs of quasilinear length (their Open Problem 1). This paper answers it for every polynomial query bound, with the simulators above in place of a strict polynomial-time perfect simulator. The proofs were developed with extensive AI assistance and have been checked by the authors. We mask the Reed-Solomon proof of proximity of Ben-Sasson and Sudan at every node of its recursion. By a locator lemma, at every node, whatever [MATH] of its proof symbols reveal about its input is determined by [MATH] input values. We prove it with the coprime-order argument of Bafna and Vyas (2026); our treatment of domain points is new. Dinur's gap amplification gives constant query complexity.
