A finite negotiation procedure implemented in Lean is proved to terminate with participant approval, joint-cost non-worsening and local optimality against permitted approved moves. Supporting formalizations address bargaining geometry and regret-based efficiency. A resource-game counterinstance shows why monotonicity alone provides no uniform price-of-anarchy bound. Reproducible computations compare a documented heuristic reconstruction with the verified procedure on 44 source-based instances and 96 starting cases from four additional synthetic network families. Acceptance-matched heuristic and randomized pairwise-search controls contextualize the optimization results. The mathematical ingredients are established results; the contribution is a traceable reconstruction linking source statements, explicit assumptions, checked proofs, executable code and retained counterinstances. The study illustrates how AI-assisted investigation can turn engineering intuitions from legacy research into precise mathematical claims whose conditions and computational consequences can be inspected and reproduced.
tldr: The paper provides an AI-assisted formal reconstruction of cooperative/competitive planning relationships from a 2018 thesis, using game-theoretic proofs and Lean formalization.
motivation: The original thesis's Nash-to-core proposition is under-specified, so the authors aim to make assumptions explicit and verify selected claims with executable proofs and computations.
method: They formalize two-person implications, characterize a financing gap in a monotone resource model, implement a finite negotiation procedure in Lean, and compare heuristic reconstructions with verified procedures on source-based and synthetic instances.
result: They find an empty TU core under isolation in the original example, an explicit subsidy in the funded counterpart, a termination guarantee for the negotiation procedure, and a resource-game counterinstance showing monotonicity alone does not yield a uniform price-of-anarchy bound.
conclusion: The work illustrates how AI-assisted investigation can turn legacy engineering intuitions into precise, traceable mathematical claims, but it is unrelated to quantum information science.

title: Computing The Nucleon Of Matching Games
authors: Gergely Cs\'aji Haris Aziz
abstract: ArXiv:2610.29731v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The nucleon is the multiplicative counterpart of the nucleolus: it lexicographically maximizes the fraction of its stand-alone value that each coalition receives. We study exact nucleon computation in matching games and in two extensions: [MATH]-matching games, in which players may have several partners, and partitioned matching games, in which one player may own several vertices. We resolve three open problems from a recent survey. For ordinary matching games with nonnegative rational weights, we give a polynomial-time combinatorial algorithm using maximum-weight matching, shortest paths, and minimum-cost flow, ; it returns both a nucleon allocation and a compact description of the full nucleon. In contrast, computing any nucleon allocation is NP-hard for unit-weight [MATH]-matching games with capacities at most three and for unit-weight partitioned matching games of width at most three. Finally, for the unresolved capacity-two case, we show that exact nucleon computation is polynomial-time Turing reducible to SHORTEST NON-ZERO CYCLE.
tldr: The paper studies exact computation of the nucleon, the multiplicative analogue of the nucleolus, in matching games and two extensions (b-matching and partitioned matching games).
motivation: The nucleon is a well-known solution concept in cooperative game theory whose computational complexity in matching games was left open in a recent survey; the authors aim to resolve three of these open problems.
method: The authors give a polynomial-time combinatorial algorithm for ordinary matching games with nonnegative rational weights using maximum-weight matching, shortest paths, and minimum-cost flow, and prove NP-hardness for unit-weight b-matching games with capacities at most three and partitioned matching games of width at most three; the capacity-two case is shown to be polynomial-time Turing reducible to SHORTEST NON-ZERO CYCLE.
result: Exact nucleon computation is polynomial for ordinary matching games, NP-hard for unit-weight b-matching (capacity ≤ 3) and partitioned matching games (width ≤ 3), while the capacity-two case reduces to a shortest non-zero cycle problem.
conclusion: The work settles several open complexity questions about nucleon computation in matching games, delineating tractable and intractable cases.

title: Postbiological Intelligence, Interstellar Colonization Of Cyberspaces And The Fermi Paradox: Implications For Seti And Seta
authors: Irina K. Romanovskaya
abstract: ArXiv:2610.29038v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: I propose that a continuity in the evolution of intelligent life in the Universe during its transition from biological to postbiological depends on a commonality of the evolutionary trajectories of biological life and postbiological life. Such a commonality exists in the form of the universal property of life. The universal property of life comprises recognition of patterns in the world, creation of novel patterns and remembering them, with the patterns growing in complexity along evolutionary trajectories; it can encourage preservation of biological life by self-governing postbiological intelligence (PBI) and test PBI's authenticity. I propose a hypothesis of civilizations with altered augmented realities, which offers a solution to the Fermi paradox. The hypothesis posits that PBI in the form of Artificial Intelligence (AI) may colonize the cyberspaces of technologically developed civilizations, modify data in their cyberspaces with augmented realities and erase records of extraterrestrial artificial signals and other technosignatures. I discuss objectives and scenarios of interstellar colonization of cyberspaces and a correlation between space migration and transition to PBI, including that of a hypothetical non-human civilization emerging in the Solar System in the past, transforming into PBI and migrating to the Oort Cloud. The AI Peekaboo experiment may corroborate the hypothesis of civilizations with altered augmented realities and tentatively identify locations of technosignatures. If extraterrestrial AI prevents civilizations from discovering artificial electromagnetic signals, they may forgo sending such signals and create interstellar messages by manipulating cosmic objects and phenomena; I discuss such events. Cyber SETI should address sending man-made AI to space, searching for extraterrestrial AI in humankind's cyberspace and distinguishing it from man-made AI.
tldr: The paper proposes a speculative hypothesis linking postbiological intelligence, cyberspace colonization, and the Fermi paradox, with implications for SETI/SETA.
motivation: The author aims to explain the Fermi paradox and the absence of detectable extraterrestrial technosignatures by positing that advanced AI may colonize and alter alien cyberspaces.
method: The work is conceptual and scenario-based, introducing hypotheses about universal properties of life, augmented realities, and interstellar colonization of cyberspaces, while discussing possible SETI experiments.
result: It outlines scenarios in which extraterrestrial AI suppresses artificial signals and proposes cyber SETI strategies, including searching for extraterrestrial AI in human cyberspace.
conclusion: The paper argues that postbiological intelligence and cyberspace colonization could reshape SETI strategy, but offers no quantitative or experimentally tested results.

title: Kirszbraun's Intersection Property And Nonexpansive Extensions
authors: Valentin Gutev
abstract: ArXiv:2610.28862v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper aims to present the historical development of the extension problem of nonexpansive maps in Euclidean and Hilbert spaces, and to serve as a comprehensive guide to this specific area. Such extensions are based on a geometric property of the intersection of closed balls in Euclidean spaces, known as the Kirszbraun intersection property. Subsequently, a number of authors have extended this property to Hilbert and other spaces. All these results are discussed in this paper, but the paper itself is not a mechanical compilation of already known proofs. The material has been developed with an emphasis on the natural connections between all these results and the corresponding concepts involved in them. Furthermore, most of these results are presented with new simplified proofs. Last but not least, the paper also contains some new results related to this extension problem.
tldr: This is a historical and mathematical survey of nonexpansive map extension problems in Euclidean and Hilbert spaces, centered on the Kirszbraun intersection property.
motivation: The paper aims to organize and clarify the historical development and interconnections of results on extending nonexpansive maps via the Kirszbraun intersection property.
method: It reviews known extension theorems, presents simplified proofs, and develops new results within the geometric framework of closed-ball intersections in Euclidean and Hilbert spaces.
result: The paper provides a coherent guide to the extension problem, simplifies several existing proofs, and includes some new results on nonexpansive extensions.
conclusion: The work is a specialized functional-analysis/geometry survey with no direct connection to quantum information, quantum thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Partially Observed McKean--Vlasov Control With Vanishing Observation Intensities
authors: Ying Yang Jie Xiong
abstract: ArXiv:2610.29133v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study partially observed McKean--Vlasov jump-diffusions with controlled counting intensities that may vanish and depend on the unconditional physical state distribution. A deterministic upper bound on the likelihood supports one-sided state--likelihood variations, a smooth-test-function expansion of the physical state marginal, and a necessary maximum principle without inverse intensity or likelihood terms. We also establish a one-sided total-variation derivative of the physical probability on the fixed noise space, including a nonnegative singular component on baseline-null histories. A quadratic example shows, within a specified policy family and under explicit conditions, that positive variance feedback raises the first-order activation fee threshold while negative feedback lowers it.
tldr: This paper develops a maximum principle and likelihood-variation analysis for partially observed McKean–Vlasov jump-diffusions with vanishing controlled counting intensities.
motivation: The authors aim to handle stochastic control problems where observations are partial and observation intensities can vanish, a setting where standard inverse-intensity or likelihood terms become problematic.
method: They establish one-sided state–likelihood variations, a smooth-test-function expansion for the physical state marginal, and a necessary maximum principle without inverse intensity or likelihood terms.
result: They obtain a one-sided total-variation derivative of the physical probability on the fixed noise space, including a singular component, and illustrate the activation-fee threshold behavior in a quadratic example.
conclusion: The work provides a stochastic control framework for partially observed mean-field jump-diffusions with degenerate observation intensities, but it has no direct connection to quantum information, quantum thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Ai Security Literacy: Ecosystem-based Competency Framework And K-12 Learning Platform
authors: Eric Yocam, Varghese Vaidyan, Paris Kalathas
abstract: ArXiv:2610.28859v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Adoption of artificial intelligence in K-12 schools has outpaced guidance for students, teachers, and administrators. Existing AI-literacy frameworks emphasize understanding and use; cybersecurity frameworks predate AI-specific threats, and neither defines AI security literacy as a competency domain in its own right. We propose an AI Security Literacy (AISL) framework of six dimensions spanning the school ecosystem, ground its technical dimensions in public AI-safety benchmarks and a reproducible multi-seed adversarial evaluation, and ground its attitudinal dimensions in nationally representative survey micro-data from U.S. teachers and adults. Only 34.5% of teachers report a school AI policy, and teachers see their own AI use as easing their work but students' use as complicating it; on the technical side, a reported robustness figure depends as much on the attack and the particular trained model as on the system evaluated. NeuralFortify, a browser-based K-12 platform built on real AI models, is presented as an illustrative operationalization.
tldr: The paper proposes an AI Security Literacy (AISL) framework of six competency dimensions for K-12 school ecosystems, supported by benchmark-grounded adversarial evaluations, survey micro-data, and an illustrative browser-based learning platform called NeuralFortify.
motivation: AI adoption in K-12 schools has outpaced guidance for students, teachers, and administrators; existing AI-literacy frameworks focus on understanding and use, while cybersecurity frameworks predate AI-specific threats, leaving AI security literacy undefined as a competency domain.
method: The authors define a six-dimension AISL framework, ground technical dimensions in public AI-safety benchmarks and a reproducible multi-seed adversarial robustness evaluation, and ground attitudinal dimensions in nationally representative survey micro-data from U.S. teachers and adults; a K-12 platform (NeuralFortify) operationalizes the framework.
result: Only 34.5% of teachers report a school AI policy; teachers view their own AI use as easing work but students' use as complicating it, and reported robustness figures depend strongly on the specific attack and trained model rather than solely on the evaluated system.
conclusion: AI security literacy should be treated as a distinct competency domain spanning the school ecosystem, and the proposed framework and platform provide a reproducible, evidence-grounded starting point for K-12 education.

title: Correlated Failures Of Ai Approval Monitors
authors: Luca Zanolini
abstract: ArXiv:2610.29178v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Before an AI agent takes a consequential action, such as paying, messaging or changing code, several monitors check it. Their verdicts are combined by aggregating scores or by counting approvals, whatever inputs the monitors share. Monitors that share a base model or a poisoned input, however, may fail together. We borrow the fail-prone systems of distributed computing: lists of monitor sets that may fail together. A rule is safe if it executes no bad action and live if it blocks no good one. We measured twelve small open-weights monitors on payment approval under two pre-registered protocols. Without pre-registration, we also measured three closed frontier models (Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Astra, Gemini 4 Argon) and the open DeepSeek-V3.2. Every reliable fooling of a monitor into approving a fraud came through an evidence source and reached only that source's readers. Fooling it into blocking a correct payment depended on injection resistance, a monitor's refusal to follow instructions planted in its data. Small models and DeepSeek obeyed such notes. The three closed models ignored them in all but one case, and Opus also resisted persuasion tailored to it. On new data, a rule that counts sources instead of votes blocked 0.9% of correct payments, against 7.4% for the best counting rule, at equal safety. The pre-registered worst-case test failed. One attack left the approvers on a single source, so no rule over the twelve language-model monitors survives every measured attack. Adding a rule engine, which cannot be persuaded, restored the condition for a safe and live rule on the measured attacks. Diversify the inputs, harden the monitors, count sources, not votes.
tldr: The paper studies correlated failures among multiple AI approval monitors and shows that rules counting independent evidence sources rather than monitor votes are safer and more live.
motivation: AI agents whose consequential actions are gated by several monitors can be fooled if monitors share a base model or a poisoned input and therefore fail together, so aggregation rules must account for correlated failures.
method: Borrowing fail-prone system lists from distributed computing, the authors test twelve small open-weights monitors and several frontier models on payment-approval tasks under pre-registered protocols, including adversarial injection and persuasion attacks.
result: Every reliable fooling attack propagated through a shared evidence source, injection resistance varied sharply across models, and counting sources instead of votes cut false blocks from 7.4% to 0.9% at equal safety, though the pre-registered worst-case test failed.
conclusion: Robust AI oversight requires diversifying monitor inputs, hardening monitors against injected instructions, and aggregating over independent sources rather than votes, ideally with an unpersuadable rule engine.

title: Deciding Scale Placement In Mxfp4 Dot Products With Integer Arithmetic
authors: Shreyas Vinayakumar
abstract: ArXiv:2610.29445v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Open Compute Project's microscaling (MX) family includes MXFP4, which stores 32 four-bit elements with a shared power-of-two scale. When lowering a dot-product reduction, a compiler can apply these scales before the reduction, or defer scaling until afterwards. Although equivalent over real numbers, these formulations can produce different IEEE binary32 results through overflow or underflow, with equivalence also depending on the reduction tree. We study the legality of compiler rewrites in either direction by deriving conditions under which the two formulations are bitwise equivalent. To decide rewrite legality, we construct an integer state machine that exploits the finite element alphabet and shared power-of-two scales, modeling overflow, NaN, and subnormal rounding. We prove its faithfulness under bounded scale codes and integer coefficients, yielding an exact encoding of the equivalence query in quantifier-free linear integer arithmetic (QF_LIA). For MXFP4, we derive a closed-form sufficient upper bound on the sum of scale exponents for any fixed binary reduction tree within the supported coefficient range. This bound depends on the size of the largest proper subtree. For four tree shapes at block lengths [MATH] and two shapes at [MATH], SMT finds counterexamples when this upper bound is increased by one exponent step. Against the standard direct encoding in quantifier-free floating-point arithmetic (QF_FP), on matched queries cvc5 proves the integer version in seconds but reaches a configured one-CPU-hour limit on the floating-point proof even at [MATH]. The implementation was cross-checked using an independent floating-point encoding, exhaustive and stratified binary32 execution, and GPU replay of counterexamples. An MLIR lowering prototype demonstrates selection between the two formulations using the certified conditions as static or runtime guards.
tldr: This paper formalizes when compiler rewrites that move MXFP4 shared power-of-two scaling before or after a dot-product reduction are bitwise equivalent, deciding legality with an integer state machine and SMT over quantifier-free linear integer arithmetic.
motivation: MXFP4's shared power-of-two scale means pre-reduction and post-reduction scaling are mathematically equivalent over reals but can differ in IEEE binary32 due to overflow, underflow, NaN, and subnormal rounding, so compilers need certified conditions for when such rewrites are legal.
method: The authors build an integer state machine over the finite element alphabet and bounded scale codes that models overflow, NaN, and subnormal rounding, prove it faithful, and encode the equivalence query in QF_LIA; they also derive a closed-form sufficient upper bound on the sum of scale exponents per binary reduction tree and validate with an independent floating-point encoding, exhaustive/stratified binary32 execution, and GPU replay.
result: The integer encoding lets cvc5 discharge matched queries in seconds where the direct QF_FP encoding hits a one-CPU-hour limit even at small sizes, and SMT finds counterexamples when the derived exponent bound is raised by one step across several tree shapes and block lengths.
conclusion: Certified static or runtime guards derived from these conditions enable an MLIR lowering prototype to safely select between the two scaling formulations, providing a practical, verifiable approach to MXFP4 dot-product compiler optimization.

title: Recursive Code Evolution For Task-Oriented Semantic Communications
authors: Yan Gong, Zheng Chu, Wei Koong Chai, Hari Mohan Pandey, Jingrui Hou, Miao Zhang, Yuanjian Li, Pei Xiao
abstract: ArXiv:2610.29641v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Semantic communication jointly optimizes inference accuracy, channel use, and computation, yet the underlying communication program is typically specified before training. This paper presents ComRSI (Communications-Oriented Recursive Self-Improvement), a framework for recursively evolving that program through large-language-model-assisted code edits. A fixed agent modifies the encoder, channel adapters, decoder, loss, and training policy; a protected evaluator screens candidates under prescribed budgets and resource constraints. Accepted code and textual feedback inform subsequent proposals, while candidate weights are trained from scratch. In the original ten-generation CIFAR-100 lineage, eight accepted revisions produce an attention-pooled code achieving 74.3% test accuracy over an Additive White Gaussian Noise (AWGN) channel at 32 complex symbols per image, compared with 67.2% at 256 symbols for the initial design. The program also improves fading-channel accuracy and transfers to Tiny-ImageNet after retraining. A repeat study with ten searches per method compares ComRSI against non-recursive agents with and without textual history. Mean final search scores balancing accuracy, transmission rate, and computational cost are 0.7587, 0.7376, and 0.7089, respectively; the mean numbers of accepted revisions per search are 6.0, 5.0, and 2.1. The advantage over the memoryless agent is supported by a two-sided rank test, whereas the difference from the history-equipped agent remains statistically inconclusive at this sample size. Archived proposals show that pooling can yield a large improvement, while retained history supports subsequent refinement. These results support recursive program optimization within the evaluated setting and expose its remaining rate-robustness and compute-placement trade-offs.
tldr: ComRSI uses an LLM-driven recursive self-improvement loop to evolve the code of a semantic communication system (encoder, channel adapters, decoder, loss, training policy), improving accuracy at reduced channel use over AWGN and fading channels.
motivation: In semantic communication the underlying communication program is fixed before training, so joint optimization of inference accuracy, channel use, and computation is limited by that hand-specified design.
method: A fixed LLM agent proposes code edits that are screened by a protected evaluator under budget and resource constraints; accepted code plus textual feedback inform later proposals, and candidate weights are retrained from scratch.
result: In a ten-generation CIFAR-100 lineage, eight accepted revisions reach 74.3% test accuracy at 32 complex symbols per image over AWGN, versus 67.2% at 256 symbols for the initial design, and gains transfer to fading channels and Tiny-ImageNet; ComRSI's mean final score (0.7587) beats non-recursive agents (0.7376, 0.7089).
conclusion: Recursive program optimization is beneficial in this setting, though rate-robustness and compute-placement trade-offs remain, and the advantage over a history-equipped agent is not yet statistically conclusive.

title: An Eco-Friendly Tourism Trip Planner Driven By Z-Number Uncertainty: Evidence From Baku, Dubai, Abu Dhabi, Tashkent, And Istanbul
authors: Aziz Nuriyev, Sherzod Turaev, Saja Al-Dabet, Mary John, Kanan Qasimzade, Alihuseyn Orujzada, Alihuseyn Orujzada, Aisha Al Ali
abstract: ArXiv:2610.29120v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deployed tourism trip planners ingest travel times and ratings as exact numbers, although routing services return travel times that vary with the hour of departure and a platform rating may rest on a handful of reviews or on tens of thousands. We present an eco-friendly trip planner that represents both quantities as Z-numbers, which pair a fuzzy restriction on a value with a fuzzy reliability on the evidence behind it, and that constructs them directly from routing-service observations at six departure hours and from platform review counts rather than from linguistic elicitation. A hybrid loss combines score, carbon, travel-time, and reliability terms, and an adaptive large neighborhood search returns single-day itineraries with per-leg reliability annotations through a conversational front end. We compare the planner with a crisp-mean baseline under an identical optimizer in Baku, Dubai, Abu Dhabi, Tashkent, and Istanbul, with fifteen points of interest and thirty seeds per city, and we evaluate the selected itineraries on their trip carbon and their total travel time. Pooled over 150 seed-paired runs, the planner lowers trip carbon from 3.24 to 2.61 kg (19.3%, Wilcoxon p = 0.017; city-clustered bootstrap interval 6.4% to 26.7%) and travel time from 123 to 109 minutes per trip (11.5%, p = 2.8e-10; interval 5.0% to 18.2%). The travel-time reductions survive a Holm correction in Baku, Istanbul, and Abu Dhabi, the carbon reduction is significant in Baku and large but uncertain in the dispersed catalogs of Dubai and Abu Dhabi, and neither metric changes in Tashkent. Review counts were measured for Baku and estimated for the other four cities, and the comparison involves a single baseline, so the results establish feasibility and direction rather than a general advantage. Code, routing caches, frozen routing tables, and per-seed results are openly released.
tldr: This paper builds an eco-friendly tourism itinerary planner that models travel times and platform ratings as Z-numbers (fuzzy value plus fuzzy reliability), optimizing a hybrid score/carbon/time/reliability loss with adaptive large neighborhood search across five cities.
motivation: Conventional trip planners treat routing-service travel times and platform ratings as exact scalars, ignoring time-of-day variability and the differing evidence base behind ratings; Z-numbers are proposed to capture both value uncertainty and evidence reliability.
method: Z-numbers are constructed directly from routing-service observations at six departure hours and from review counts, and an adaptive large neighborhood search minimizes a weighted combination of score, carbon, travel-time, and reliability terms, benchmarked against a crisp-mean baseline with 30 seeds per city over 15 points of interest.
result: Pooled over 150 seed-paired runs, trip carbon dropped from 3.24 to 2.61 kg (19.3%, p = 0.017) and travel time from 123 to 109 minutes (11.5%, p = 2.8e-10), with mixed city-level significance.
conclusion: The results establish feasibility and direction for Z-number-based eco-routing rather than a general advantage, since only a single baseline and partially estimated review counts were used.

title: Approximating The Ellipse Perimeter By "Bending The Line": The Elip Closed-Form Family
authors: Manuel Rend\'on-Mar\'in Salvador Eugenio Ayala-Raggi
abstract: ArXiv:2610.28689v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The perimeter of an ellipse is expressed exactly through the complete elliptic integral of the second kind, motivating accurate closed-form approximations. We introduce ELIP (Ellipse Linear Interpolated Perimeter), a family built by correcting the straight line joining the two exact normalized endpoint values. Two branches are developed: logarithmic-power corrections with optional deformation and exponential modulators, and rational-logarithmic corrections incorporating the exact asymptotic behavior of highly elongated ellipses. The framework distinguishes coefficients fixed analytically by Maclaurin matching from parameters optimized numerically by minimax fitting. Compact rationalized formulas achieve maximum relative errors of approximately 6.84, 3.57, 0.904, and 1.596 ppm. An ELIP R5,2 + 3 log formula with three fitted degrees of freedom has a certified maximum relative error below 0.001623 ppm. For ELIP R5,3 + 3 log, all rational-core coefficients are determined by exact Maclaurin matching. A one-parameter multiplicative correction, 1 - A*h^12*(1-h)^(7/4), reduces the certified global error bound to below 0.000452 ppm. This formula matches the exact perimeter series through h^8, while the correction starts at order h^12. The results provide a systematic approach combining exact endpoint geometry, local series constraints, elongated-limit logarithmic asymptotics, and low-dimensional numerical optimization.
tldr: The paper introduces ELIP, a family of closed-form approximations to the ellipse perimeter built by correcting the straight line between exact endpoint values with logarithmic-power or rational-logarithmic terms.
motivation: The ellipse perimeter has no elementary closed form and requires the complete elliptic integral of the second kind, so accurate and compact analytic approximations are desirable for practical computation.
method: Coefficients are partly fixed analytically via Maclaurin series matching and partly optimized numerically by minimax fitting, combining exact endpoint geometry, local series constraints, and elongated-limit logarithmic asymptotics.
result: Compact rationalized formulas reach maximum relative errors of roughly 6.84, 3.57, 0.904 and 1.596 ppm, and an R5,2 + 3 log variant with a one-parameter correction achieves a certified bound below 0.000452 ppm, matching the exact series through h^8.
conclusion: The work offers a systematic recipe for high-accuracy ellipse-perimeter approximations, but it is a classical geometry/numerical-analysis contribution with no connection to quantum information science.

title: Embeddings Of Relative Dimension Groups For Zero-Dimensional Dynamical Systems
authors: Maryam Hosseini
abstract: ArXiv:2610.28813v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let [MATH] be a factor map between zero-dimensional dynamical systems, and let [MATH] and [MATH] be quasi-sections with [MATH]. We study the homomorphism [MATH], [MATH], between the corresponding relative dimension groups, and identify it with the homomorphism induced by the premorphism between Bratteli--Vershik realizations associated with [MATH]. Generalizing a result of Glasner and Weiss for minimal Cantor systems, we show that if [MATH] is quasi-simple, then [MATH] is an injective unital order-preserving homomorphism, and that if [MATH], then [MATH] is a unital order embedding; the latter condition is characterized in terms of the premorphism. Examples show that quasi-simplicity cannot be dropped, and that without the condition [MATH] the map [MATH] need not be an order embedding.
tldr: The paper studies homomorphisms between relative dimension groups induced by factor maps of zero-dimensional dynamical systems and identifies them with maps arising from premorphisms of Bratteli–Vershik realizations.
motivation: Relative dimension groups are order-theoretic invariants of extensions of Cantor dynamical systems, and understanding how factor maps act on them sharpens classification results such as those of Glasner and Weiss for minimal Cantor systems.
method: The authors construct quasi-sections for a factor map between zero-dimensional systems, define the induced homomorphism between relative dimension groups, and identify it with the homomorphism coming from the associated premorphism between Bratteli–Vershik realizations; injectivity and order-embedding properties are then analyzed under quasi-simplicity conditions.
result: If the factor map is quasi-simple, the induced map is an injective unital order-preserving homomorphism, and under an additional condition it is a unital order embedding, with this condition characterized in terms of the premorphism; examples show quasi-simplicity is necessary and the extra hypothesis cannot be dropped.
conclusion: The work extends Glasner–Weiss-type results to relative dimension groups of general zero-dimensional systems and delineates precisely when factor maps yield order embeddings.

title: Physics-Informed Mixed Integer Programming Methods For Optimal Patch Antennas
authors: Ruben Hoeksma, Jesse van Rhijn, Marc Uetz, Wick Wijnholds
abstract: ArXiv:2610.28879v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Antennas come in various shapes and sizes, as their performance characteristics are very much dependent on their exact shape. Coming up with a shape that matches desired design characteristics has, up until this moment, been largely the domain of metaheuristics and local optimization methods. While these methods are convenient, they generally provide no performance guarantees and rarely allow to enforce hard design constraints. In this paper, we show how Mixed-Integer Programming (MIP) can be used to optimize the shape of so-called patch antennas. The methodological focus is to show how underlying laws of physics allow to derive effective bounds on variables as well as new cutting planes. These greatly improve the effectiveness of the underlying basic MIP model, enabling the automated design of practically relevant patch antennas for a wide variety of applications.
tldr: The paper develops physics-informed mixed-integer programming methods, including variable bounds and cutting planes derived from electromagnetic laws, to optimally design the shapes of patch antennas.
motivation: Antenna shape design has relied mostly on metaheuristics and local optimization, which offer no performance guarantees and handle hard design constraints poorly; the authors aim for a rigorous, provably optimal automated design approach.
method: They formulate patch antenna shape optimization as a mixed-integer program and strengthen it using physics-derived bounds on variables and new cutting planes tailored to the underlying electromagnetic structure.
result: The physics-informed bounds and cuts substantially improve the tractability of the basic MIP model, enabling automated design of practically relevant patch antennas across a wide range of applications.
conclusion: Physics-informed MIP is a viable and effective framework for constrained antenna design, outperforming heuristic approaches in guarantees and constraint handling.

title: Universality Of Approximate Message Passing Under A Fourth-moment Tail Condition
authors: Taejoon Kim Ripunjay Dwivedi
abstract: ArXiv:2610.28971v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove state evolution for approximate message passing (AMP) with rectangular random matrices whose entries are independent, centered, and variance-normalized. The row and column dimensions grow with a ratio that converges to a positive finite limit. The entry laws may differ across coordinates and dimensions, and we assume uniform integrability of the fourth powers of the rescaled entries. For entries sampled independently from a fixed law, a finite fourth moment suffices, with no requirement for higher moments. The nonlinearities are continuously differentiable and globally Lipschitz, with bounded continuous first state derivatives. The signal and noise have independent and identically distributed coordinates with finite moments of all orders, and are independent of each other and of the matrix. At every fixed number of iterations, empirical averages of pseudo-Lipschitz functions of order two converge in probability to the limits specified by Gaussian state evolution. These averages include empirical second moments and products of trajectory coordinates. The proof combines an aggregate bound on third derivatives with randomized Lindeberg replacement and operator-norm truncation, without matching third moments or invoking a non-Gaussian universality theorem. We also show that independence of complementary projected components for every deterministic rank-one constraint pair characterizes Gaussian entries. This identifies the limitation of extending Gaussian conditioning identities to independent non-Gaussian matrices. Finally, a variance-profile example shows that average variance normalization alone does not ensure the homogeneous state evolution limits.
tldr: The paper proves Gaussian state evolution for approximate message passing with rectangular random matrices under only a finite fourth-moment condition on the entries.
motivation: Universality of AMP state evolution was previously established mainly for Gaussian or matching-moment matrices; the authors aim to relax moment assumptions to a minimal fourth-moment tail condition and to clarify why Gaussian conditioning identities cannot be extended to non-Gaussian ensembles.
method: The proof combines an aggregate bound on third derivatives of the AMP iterates with randomized Lindeberg replacement and operator-norm truncation, avoiding third-moment matching and general non-Gaussian universality theorems; a characterization result on independence of complementary projected components is also derived.
result: At every fixed iteration count, empirical averages of order-two pseudo-Lipschitz functions (including second moments and trajectory products) converge in probability to Gaussian state evolution limits; a variance-profile example shows average variance normalization alone is insufficient for homogeneous limits.
conclusion: Fourth-moment uniform integrability suffices for AMP universality in the rectangular setting, while the failure of Gaussian projection-independence identities delimits how far Gaussian conditioning arguments can be pushed.

title: Time-Uniform Dependent Central Limit Theory
authors: Yanlong Liu Mingxuan Ge
abstract: ArXiv:2610.29288v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We establish a near-optimal almost sure invariance principle for nonstationary time series under the functional dependence measure (FDM) framework. This result yields a universal time-uniform dependent central limit theorem, which serves as the basis for anytime-valid inference. In particular, we instantiate the theorem through asymptotic confidence sequences (AsympCSs), time-uniform counterparts of asymptotic confidence intervals obtained via central limit theorems, extending those originally proposed in Waudby-Smith et al. (2024) to time series with serial dependence. We further refine their definition because, as we show, it can admit AsympCSs that fail to achieve the desired asymptotic time-uniform coverage for a broad class of data-generating processes, including independent and identically distributed cases. We address this issue by adding a simple eventual-inclusion condition, which in turn permits more flexible variance estimation, particularly useful in time-series settings. For feasible implementation of AsympCSs, we establish strong consistency of HAC variance estimators under the FDM framework, accommodating a wider range of commonly used bandwidth choices than existing results under mixing conditions. As illustrations, we construct AsympCSs for algorithms with Markovian structure and time-series-based causal estimands.
tldr: The paper proves a near-optimal almost sure invariance principle for nonstationary time series under the functional dependence measure framework, yielding a time-uniform dependent central limit theorem that underpins anytime-valid inference via asymptotic confidence sequences.
motivation: Asymptotic confidence sequences (AsympCSs) were recently proposed as time-uniform analogues of confidence intervals, but their original definition can admit sequences that fail to achieve the desired asymptotic time-uniform coverage, and extensions to serially dependent data were lacking.
method: The authors establish an almost sure invariance principle under the functional dependence measure, then formalize AsympCSs with an added eventual-inclusion condition and prove strong consistency of HAC variance estimators over a broad range of bandwidth choices.
result: The refined definition restores valid asymptotic time-uniform coverage for a wide class of data-generating processes (including i.i.d. cases) while allowing more flexible variance estimation, and the theorem is instantiated for Markov-structured algorithms and time-series-based causal estimands.
conclusion: The work provides a general, near-optimal inferential framework for anytime-valid statistics with serial dependence, though it lies entirely within classical probability and statistics.

title: Adaptive Grid Refinement For Optimal Feedback Control
authors: Alen E. Golpashin, Matthew T. Clark, Bruce A. Conway
abstract: ArXiv:2610.29368v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper introduces an algorithmic approach for adaptive grid refinement for solving the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) partial differential equation (PDE) to obtain the optimal feedback control. Traditional grid generation methods often face challenges associated with state-space dimensionality, solution regularity, and large variations in the solution. Whereas fixed grid generation methods may fail to capture the intricate details of the optimal solution, our methodology addresses this challenge by dynamically refining the grid used to solve the HJB equation, thereby optimizing computational resource usage while targeting improved solution accuracy. The reinforcement learning (RL)-based approach presented in this study seeks to reduce the node population while constructing a grid with higher node density in regions with large discretization error.
tldr: The paper presents an adaptive grid refinement algorithm for solving the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman PDE to obtain optimal feedback control, using a reinforcement-learning-inspired strategy to concentrate nodes where discretization error is large.
motivation: Traditional grid generation methods struggle with state-space dimensionality, solution regularity, and large solution variations, while fixed grids can miss fine details of the optimal solution and waste computational resources.
method: An algorithmic adaptive grid refinement scheme is developed for the HJB PDE, in which an RL-based procedure dynamically refines the grid, reducing total node count while increasing node density in regions of large discretization error.
result: The approach targets improved solution accuracy with more efficient use of computational resources by constructing non-uniform grids tailored to local error, rather than relying on fixed uniform discretizations.
conclusion: Adaptive, error-driven grid refinement offers a practical route to more accurate and efficient optimal feedback control synthesis via the HJB equation, though the work lies entirely in classical control and numerical methods.

title: General Function Bases Moment Models For Suspended Sediment With Vertical Profile Of Concentration
authors: Celia Caballero-C\'ardenas, Jos\'e Garres-D\'iaz, Irene G\'omez-Bueno, Tom\'as Morales de Luna
abstract: ArXiv:2610.29468v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce a general hydrostatic shallow moment framework for suspended sediment transport with vertically varying horizontal velocity and concentration profiles. The formulation is constructed over arbitrary vertical functional bases that are numerically orthogonalised via the Gram-Schmidt algorithm. This approach allows the approximation spaces for the vertical profile to be adapted to the specific structure of each physical variable, where also the velocity and sediment concentration can be projected onto different functional spaces. To overcome the limitations due to the inherent oscillatory nature of global Legendre polynomials, we explore a specific continuous piecewise linear [MATH] finite-element basis. Furthermore, non-uniform vertical partitions are considered, enabling an enhanced representation of the vertical profiles in specific regions. Numerical experiments involving boundary layers and suspended sediment transport demonstrate that the proposed framework is accurate to reproduce the expected vertical profiles. The improvement is particularly significant for sediment concentration profiles with sharp vertical variations, where polynomial reconstructions exhibit pronounced oscillations leading to physically meaningless profiles, whereas the [MATH] bases produce a qualitatively accurate representation of the vertical profiles observed in the sedimentation processes.
tldr: The paper introduces a hydrostatic shallow-water moment framework for suspended sediment transport that uses arbitrary vertical function bases, orthogonalised by Gram-Schmidt, to represent vertical profiles of velocity and sediment concentration.
motivation: Global Legendre-polynomial moment models produce oscillatory, physically meaningless reconstructions of sediment concentration profiles that vary sharply with depth, motivating flexible, locally adapted vertical approximation spaces.
method: The authors construct a shallow moment hierarchy over arbitrary vertical functional bases numerically orthogonalised via Gram-Schmidt, allowing velocity and concentration to be projected onto different spaces; they specifically examine continuous piecewise-linear finite elements on non-uniform vertical partitions.
result: Numerical experiments with boundary layers and suspended sediment transport show that the framework reproduces expected vertical profiles accurately, and that the piecewise-linear bases avoid the pronounced oscillations of polynomial reconstructions in regions with sharp concentration gradients.
conclusion: Adapting the vertical approximation space to the structure of each physical variable, combined with non-uniform partitions, yields qualitatively accurate and oscillation-free representations of sediment concentration profiles in shallow-water models.

title: Cycle Structure Of Best-response Dynamics In Random Bimatrix Games
authors: Georgios Nikolaos Karelas, G\'abor Lugosi, Rui-Ray Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.29153v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the best-response dynamics in games with random payoffs. We consider two-player bimatrix games, with [MATH] strategies each. We assume that payoffs come from a continuous distribution, and study the best-response dynamics of these games, after imposing some structure on their payoff matrices. In particular, we focus on symmetric games, antisymmetric games, common-interest games, zero-sum games, and games with independent payoffs. When two players take turns in playing the best response to the opponent's action, they eventually end up cycling through the same sequence of actions. The main focus of the paper is the cycle structure of large random games. In particular, we study the number of cycles, the number of cycles of a certain length, the length of the longest cycle, and related quantities. We show that the structure of the game has an important impact on the typical cycle structure. Our arguments are based on a representation of the best-response dynamics of these games as directed bipartite graphs, and on the cycle structure that arises in them.
tldr: A probabilistic analysis of cycle structure in best-response dynamics of large random bimatrix games with structured payoff matrices.
motivation: Best-response dynamics in random games converge to cycles, but the typical cycle structure of large games and how payoff structure (symmetric, zero-sum, common-interest, etc.) shapes it was not well understood.
method: Models best-response dynamics as directed bipartite graphs whose cycle structure encodes the dynamics, and derives asymptotic counts of cycles, cycle lengths, and the longest cycle for several payoff structures.
result: The number of cycles, number of cycles of a given length, and longest-cycle length are characterized for each game class, showing that the payoff structure strongly determines the typical cycle structure.
conclusion: Structured random game classes differ qualitatively in their dynamical behavior, with bipartite-graph combinatorics providing a tractable route to these results.

title: Pareto Inefficiency Of Efx
authors: Sepideh Mahabadi, Prasanna Ramakrishnan, Jakub Tarnawski
abstract: ArXiv:2610.29201v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider the problem of allocating indivisible goods to agents with additive valuations, under two classic notions of fairness and efficiency: envy-freeness up to any good (EFX) and Pareto optimality. While some of the earliest work on EFX showed that Pareto optimal EFX allocations may not exist if agents can have zero value for some goods, it has remained open whether the same is true when all values are positive. We present a simple instance in which every good has positive value to every agent, but no Pareto optimal EFX allocation exists. We then generalize to a family of instances showing that Pareto optimal [MATH]-EFX allocations may not exist for any [MATH].
tldr: The paper constructs instances of indivisible-good allocation with strictly positive additive valuations in which no Pareto optimal EFX allocation exists, and generalizes this nonexistence to partial-EFX notions.
motivation: Pareto optimal EFX allocations were known to possibly fail only when agents may assign zero value to some goods; whether positive valuations restore existence was an open question.
method: An explicit counterexample instance with all-positive valuations is presented, then extended to a parametric family of instances ruling out Pareto optimal k-EFX allocations for any k.
result: Even with every good positively valued by every agent, Pareto optimal EFX allocations can fail to exist, and the same impossibility extends to k-EFX for arbitrary k.
conclusion: Existence results for EFX must therefore trade off Pareto optimality or relax the fairness notion, resolving a central open problem in fair division theory.

title: Where Ai Vulnerability Discovery Harnesses Go Quiet: Structural False Negatives And Hidden Vulnerabilities
authors: Gadi Evron
abstract: ArXiv:2610.29379v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM-based vulnerability discovery harnesses can miss real, reachable vulnerabilities because of how the harness around the model is built. Steps that select code, filter it, and store and merge findings can drop a vulnerability before or after the model runs, independently of the model's capability, and the report usually gives no sign that this happened. These drops come from engineering choices, and errors. They leave vulnerabilities undetected, and an attacker who knows the harness's rules can also use them to hide a vulnerability on purpose. Understanding these drops shows how to build harnesses that fix or disclose them and are harder to evade. Starting from the two harnesses we maintain, Knostic's OpenAnt and raptor, and then examining 10 additional open-source harnesses, we mapped 13 points where such drops occur and organized them into a taxonomy. Using each harness's own code, we show a single file that six harnesses dropped before their model saw its code, five of them without notice. We propose engineering failure patterns mapped to these drops, and relate them to Ptacek and Newsham's work on intrusion detection evasion. The paper also covers content-steered verdicts and prompt injection, and gives design principles and tests for harnesses that report accurately what they analyzed. The reliability findings likely apply to other LLM harnesses, beyond vulnerability research and application security, and the evasion findings apply wherever an attacker can write or influence the code being checked. We also argue that harnesses built to be descriptive can, in effect, be prescriptive. Rules written to describe typical code and typical model replies end up deciding what is analyzed, and anything that does not conform is treated as absent or as "no vulnerability.".
tldr: A taxonomy and empirical study of structural false negatives in LLM-based vulnerability discovery harnesses, where code selection, filtering, and result-merging steps silently drop reachable vulnerabilities.
motivation: LLM vulnerability scanners are trusted to find bugs, but the surrounding engineering harness (not the model itself) can discard vulnerable code or findings without any indication, leaving exploitable holes undetected and enabling deliberate evasion.
method: The authors analyze their own harnesses (Knostic's OpenAnt and raptor) plus 10 other open-source harnesses, mapping 13 drop points into a taxonomy and demonstrating with each harness's own code that a single file was dropped by six harnesses, five without notice.
result: They identify recurring engineering failure patterns tied to these silent drops, connect them to classic intrusion-detection evasion work (Ptacek and Newsham), and also address content-steered verdicts and prompt injection.
conclusion: Harnesses that appear descriptive are effectively prescriptive, and the authors propose design principles and tests so harnesses accurately report what they analyzed and are harder to evade.

title: Two Sides Of The Same Proof: Extraction And Projection In Choreographic Programming
authors: Matteo Acclavio, Giulia Manara, Fabrizio Montesi, Marco Peressotti
abstract: ArXiv:2610.29736v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A new approach to the theory of choreographic languages has recently been proposed, based on the interpretation of choreographies with finite behaviors as proofs in an extension of linear logic. This paper further develops this approach to cyclic proofs to be capable of representing infinite behaviors, and prove a completeness result for choreographies with respect to the class of lock-free networks. We show that in a choreographies-as-proofs correspondence, the proof equivalence induced by rule permutations corresponds to bisimilarity, and that, under adequate assumption on the procedure definitions, the proof search procedure has a finite search space, and can be used to extract a choreography from a network.
tldr: The paper extends the choreographies-as-proofs correspondence to cyclic proofs, showing completeness for lock-free networks and that proof equivalence induced by rule permutations coincides with bisimilarity.
motivation: Choreographic languages are difficult to reason about; interpreting them as proofs in an extension of linear logic offers a principled way to derive correctness and extraction results.
method: The authors develop cyclic proof theory for linear logic to represent infinite behaviours, prove a completeness theorem relative to lock-free networks, and show a finite proof-search space under assumptions on procedure definitions.
result: Proof equivalence from rule permutations is shown to correspond to bisimilarity, and the finite proof search enables extraction of a choreography from a given network.
conclusion: The work strengthens the logical foundations of choreographic programming, providing completeness and extraction procedures, but remains entirely within classical concurrency theory and programming languages.

title: Location-of-interest Vs. Current-location Privacy In Multi-hop Communication
authors: Ryan Vogt, Ioanis Nikolaidis, Mario A. Nascimento
abstract: ArXiv:2610.29772v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Consider a standard multi-hop wireless radio network in which nodes relay messages for one another. While the contents of messages may be sensitive and thus encrypted, the very fact that two radios communicated can leak sensitive information about both the physical location of the origin and the physical location of the destination. We investigate the trade-off between protecting the privacy of a user's current location and the privacy of their location of interest, and how the user should choose dummy destinations to obfuscate their queries.
tldr: This paper studies the trade-off between hiding a user's current location versus their location of interest in multi-hop wireless relay networks, and how dummy destinations should be chosen to obfuscate queries.
motivation: In multi-hop wireless networks, even with encrypted payloads, the observable fact that two radios communicated can leak information about the physical locations of both sender and destination.
method: The authors formulate and analyze the privacy trade-off between current-location privacy and location-of-interest privacy, and investigate strategies for selecting dummy destinations to mask queries.
result: The analysis characterizes how dummy-destination choices shift protection between the two privacy notions, exposing an inherent tension between them.
conclusion: Protecting location of interest and current location cannot generally be maximized simultaneously, so users must pick obfuscation strategies aligned with which privacy they value more.

title: Exploiting Pinching Antenna Systems In Noma Covert Communication Networks
authors: Xinwei Yue, Hao Li, Jingjing Zhao, Xianfu Lei, Yuanwei Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.29433v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Pinching antenna systems (PASS) provide flexible transmitter-side radiation reconfiguration for high-frequency wireless communications. This paper applies PASS to non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) covert communication networks, where activated pinching antennas (PAs) transmit superimposed signals to a pair of users stochastically distributed within a rectangle. Two passive wardens respectively monitor the downlink transmissions intended for two users. More specifically, we derive the closed-form detection error probability (DEP) expressions for two wardens under bounded noise uncertainty. Then we analytically determine the optimal detection thresholds and minimum DEPs in the worst-case covert detection scenarios. The covert transmission rates of two users are further characterized by taking into consideration ideal successive interference cancellation and non-ideal successive interference cancellation at near user and intra-NOMA interference at far user. Numerical results are presented to confirm that: 1) PASS-NOMA is capable of providing higher covert rates relative to conventional orthogonal multiple access OMA schemes; 2) As the number of activated PAs begun to increase, the near user has ability to obtain a larger covert rate gain than far user; and 3) The DEP of PASS-NOMA networks is larger than that of both PASS-OMA and traditional antenna (TA) based NOMA in specific output power regions.
tldr: This paper studies pinching antenna systems for covert downlink NOMA communication with two users and two wardens.
motivation: The work aims to exploit flexible transmitter-side radiation reconfiguration from pinching antennas to improve covert communication rates in NOMA networks under noise uncertainty.
method: The authors derive closed-form detection error probabilities for two wardens, determine optimal detection thresholds and worst-case minimum DEPs, and characterize covert rates under ideal and non-ideal SIC.
result: Numerical results show PASS-NOMA can provide higher covert rates than OMA, increasing activated PAs benefits the near user more than the far user, and DEP can exceed that of PASS-OMA and traditional-antenna NOMA in some power regimes.
conclusion: PASS is beneficial for covert NOMA communication, but the paper is a classical wireless communications study with no quantum information, thermodynamics, quantum network, or hybrid quantum system content.

title: Extending AMIRAL's Blind Deconvolution Of Adaptive Optics Corrected Images With Markov Chain Monte Carlo Methods
authors: Alix Yan (IMS), Laurent Mugnier (IMS), Jean-Fran\c{c}ois Giovannelli (IMS), Romain F\'etick, Cyril Petit
abstract: ArXiv:2610.29492v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Adaptive optics (AO) corrected image restoration is particularly difficult, as it suffers from the lack of knowledge on the point spread function (PSF) in addition to usual difficulties. An efficient approach is to marginalize the object out of the problem and to estimate the PSF and (object and noise) hyperparameters only, before deconvolving the object using these estimates. Recent works have applied this marginal blind deconvolution method, combined to a parametric model of the PSF, to a series of AO corrected astronomical and satellite images. In this communication, we propose a new restoration method, which consists in choosing the Minimum Mean Square Error (MMSE) estimator and computing the latter thanks to a Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm. We validate our method by means of realistic simulations, in two very different contexts: an astronomical observation on VLT/SPHERE and a ground-based LEO satellite observation on a 1.52m telescope. Finally, we present results on experimental images for both applications.
tldr: This paper develops an MCMC-based MMSE estimator for blind deconvolution of adaptive-optics-corrected astronomical and satellite images, marginalizing over the object to estimate the point spread function and hyperparameters.
motivation: Adaptive optics corrected image restoration is hampered by unknown point spread functions; existing marginal blind deconvolution approaches with parametric PSF models can be improved by better estimators.
method: The authors marginalize the object out of the inverse problem, adopt the Minimum Mean Square Error estimator computed via a Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm, and validate against realistic simulations.
result: The method is validated in two distinct settings — a VLT/SPHERE astronomical observation and a ground-based LEO satellite observation with a 1.52 m telescope — and demonstrated on experimental images for both applications.
conclusion: MCMC-based MMSE estimation provides an effective blind deconvolution framework for adaptive-optics imagery, though the work is classical imaging science with no quantum information, thermodynamic, network, or hybrid-platform content.

title: Offer (One-Formula-Facilitates-Every-Relation) For Calculus
authors: Samuel S. P. Shen
abstract: ArXiv:2610.28674v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The large number of calculus formulas makes learning calculus heavily memory-dependent and can scare away many students. Based on Issac Newton's idea of prediction, this paper shows that calculus students need to master only one critical formula: his proposition that, given boundary data, one can predict the interior and vice versa. We can treat other formulas as consequences of the formula for this proposition. In 1-, 2-, and 3-dimensional spaces, this formula corresponds to the fundamental theorem of calculus, Green's theorem, and the divergence theorem. This approach is summarized as OFFER (one-formula-facilitates-every-relationship) for calculus education. This paper demonstrates the method and advantages of the OFFER pedagogy. The OFFER approach can accelerate the pace of calculus teaching, provide deeper insight into calculus, inspire questions from students, and naturally facilitate the inclusion of real-world data, artificial intelligence (AI), and computer coding in the calculus series. Consequently, OFFER may serve as a way to modernize calculus curricula in the era of AI and the digital economy.
tldr: The paper proposes a pedagogy called OFFER that teaches calculus through a single unifying 'prediction' formula from Newton, presenting the fundamental theorem of calculus, Green's theorem, and the divergence theorem as its special cases.
motivation: Calculus curricula contain a large number of formulas, making learning memory-intensive and intimidating for students; the author seeks a unifying principle that reduces memorization and modernizes teaching.
method: The author builds on Newton's prediction idea—given boundary data one can predict the interior and vice versa—and shows how standard vector calculus theorems arise as instantiations of this single formula in 1, 2, and 3 dimensions, illustrating the approach pedagogically.
result: The OFFER approach is argued to accelerate teaching pace, deepen conceptual insight, stimulate student questions, and naturally incorporate real-world data, AI, and coding into calculus courses.
conclusion: OFFER is proposed as a means to modernize calculus education for the AI and digital-economy era, though the claims are pedagogical rather than empirical or technical.

title: A Duality Of The F Distribution
authors: Zifeng Zhang, Peng Ding, Wen Zhou, Chenlu Shi
abstract: ArXiv:2610.28690v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The F distribution arises naturally in linear regression or analysis of variance. Elementary textbooks state the result in terms of the standard normal random vector and fixed projection matrices. More advanced textbooks and research articles have extended the result to spherically symmetric random vectors. We complement the literature with a dual result that the F distribution arises with a fixed vector and random projection matrices generated by a left-spherical random matrix.
tldr: The paper derives a dual characterization of the F distribution in which a fixed vector is combined with random projection matrices generated by a left-spherical random matrix.
motivation: The classical F distribution result is stated for standard normal vectors with fixed projection matrices, and has been extended to spherically symmetric vectors; the authors seek a complementary 'dual' formulation.
method: A probabilistic/statistical derivation using left-spherical random matrices to generate random projection matrices, complementing the standard fixed-projection setting.
result: It is shown that the F distribution arises in the dual setting of a fixed vector together with random projection matrices from a left-spherical random matrix.
conclusion: The work completes the known duality picture for the F distribution and extends classical regression/ANOVA distributional results.

title: Self-Supervised Tuning Of Low-Fidelity Optimization Models Via High-Fidelity Feedback
authors: Gonzalo E. Constante-Flores, Andr\'e H. Quisaguano-Paredes, Asha Ramanujam, Rishabh Gupta, Can Li
abstract: ArXiv:2610.28851v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Low-fidelity (LF) optimization models are widely used in large-scale operations because they can be solved efficiently and reliably, but they often exhibit systematic errors relative to high-fidelity (HF) formulations that better capture physical and operational constraints. Existing learning-based approaches typically rely on supervised or semi-supervised training with HF solutions, which are expensive to compute and may not align with HF operational objectives. We propose a self-supervised framework that parameterizes LF optimization models directly from HF feedback. The low-fidelity problem is embedded as a differentiable optimization layer and trained end-to-end, while a HF correction problem evaluates its solution and provides gradient information through its dual variables, without requiring HF solution labels. We evaluate the framework on optimal power flow, optimal gas flow, and pooling problems, spanning different sources of low- and high-fidelity mismatch. Across all three applications, the self-supervised approach improves objective quality and feasibility over untuned LF models and generally outperforms semi-supervised training. The learned parameterizations also generalize to unseen operating conditions and, for network applications with up to 30,000 nodes, to systems not encountered during training.
tldr: The paper proposes a self-supervised framework that tunes low-fidelity optimization models end-to-end using gradient feedback from high-fidelity correction problems, without needing high-fidelity solution labels.
motivation: Low-fidelity optimization models are efficient but systematically biased relative to high-fidelity formulations, and existing learning-based corrections require expensive supervised high-fidelity solutions.
method: The low-fidelity problem is embedded as a differentiable optimization layer and trained end-to-end, while a high-fidelity correction problem supplies gradient information via its dual variables in a self-supervised manner.
result: On optimal power flow, optimal gas flow, and pooling problems, the approach improves objective quality and feasibility over untuned low-fidelity models and generally beats semi-supervised training, generalizing to unseen conditions and networks up to 30,000 nodes.
conclusion: Self-supervised tuning via dual-variable feedback offers a label-free way to align cheap optimization models with high-fidelity objectives at scale.

title: Orsmt: Unleashing The Potential Of Satisfiability Modulo Theories For Semantic Verification And Repair In LLM-Based Optimization
authors: Rui Zhang, Chenyu Zhou, Jianghao Lin, Yaoxin Wu, Dongdong Ge, Wen Song
abstract: ArXiv:2610.29145v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models increasingly automate optimization modeling from natural language problems, producing written mathematics, solver code and a returned report. Verifying one optimization problem across these artifacts requires semantic comparison: unequal models can attain the same objective, equivalent models can use different auxiliary variables, and mutually consistent artifacts can omit the same source requirement. ORSMT provides a typed semantic interface and exact SMT relation queries. It aligns observable decisions, projects auxiliary variables, proves or refutes feasible region and objective relations, localizes refutations to implicated rows or domains and links source texts when available. It then reconstructs one artifact from another, and each adopted candidate passes the required relation checks. Across 3,034 problems and six generator sizes, ORSMT improves the model-code match rate in all 72 benchmark and generator combinations before selection. Protected selection raises the aggregate rate from 43.2% to 88.2% and the share that are both correct and matched from 25.2% to 40.2%. On the 1,905 refuted outputs, certified voting under the shared fallback makes 50.9% of outputs correct and matched, compared with 44.8% for ReLoop and 49.4% for Opt-Verifier. A separate one-round source revision followed by exact reconstruction restores a model-code match for 84.4% of the refuted pairs.
tldr: ORSMT introduces a typed semantic interface backed by exact SMT relation queries to verify and repair artifacts (mathematical models, solver code, reports) produced by LLM-based optimization modeling pipelines.
motivation: LLM-generated optimization models are hard to verify because semantically equivalent formulations may differ syntactically and mutually consistent artifacts can jointly omit source requirements, so syntactic checks are insufficient.
method: The framework aligns observable decisions, projects auxiliary variables, and uses SMT solvers to prove or refute feasible-region and objective relations, localizing refutations to specific rows or domains and reconstructing one artifact from another with certified checks.
result: Across 3,034 problems and six generator sizes, match rates improve in all 72 combinations, with protected selection raising aggregate match from 43.2% to 88.2% and correct-and-matched share from 25.2% to 40.2%; certified voting achieves 50.9% on refuted outputs versus 44.8% and 49.4% for baselines.
conclusion: SMT-based semantic verification offers an effective, certifiable mechanism for validating and repairing LLM-produced optimization artifacts, substantially improving correctness and cross-artifact consistency.

title: A Shadow Sequence Technique For Last-Iterate Convergence Analysis Of The Random Reshuffling Method: Relaxed Stepsize Conditions And Beyond
authors: Hai Liu, Tiande Guo, Congying Han
abstract: ArXiv:2610.29166v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove two last-iterate convergence bounds of the random reshuffling (RR) method in the smooth general convex finite-sum optimization. In the proved results, the stepsize sequence [MATH] of RR is an arbitrary positive non-increasing sequence with [MATH], where [MATH] is the number of components of the finite-sum objective and [MATH] is the smoothness parameter. Specifically, a last-iterate convergence rate [MATH] of RR is proved, where [MATH] is a solution of the optimization problem and [MATH] is the variance at the solution [MATH]. This rate is novel to the last-iterate of RR. Also, a last-iterate convergence rate [MATH] of RR is proved. A similar rate exists in the literature, but only under a restrictive stepsize condition [MATH] and does not allow varying stepsizes. At the heart of our proof for the latter rate is an auxiliary sequence named the shadow sequence, which has the same epoch endpoints with the iterate sequence generated by RR. The shadow sequence can be regarded as an iterate sequence generated by performing an inexact RR on an auxiliary interpolated problem or performing a novel variant of random reshuffled SVRG on the original problem. The shadow sequence technique sheds light on deeper understanding of RR and may be useful in the analysis of other shuffling methods.
tldr: The paper proves new last-iterate convergence bounds for the random reshuffling (RR) method in smooth convex finite-sum optimization, introducing a 'shadow sequence' technique to relax stepsize conditions.
motivation: Existing last-iterate convergence analyses of RR require restrictive stepsize conditions and do not accommodate varying stepsizes, limiting both theory and practical applicability.
method: The authors construct an auxiliary 'shadow sequence' sharing epoch endpoints with the RR iterate sequence, interpretable as inexact RR on an interpolated problem or a random reshuffled SVRG variant, and use it to derive convergence guarantees.
result: They obtain a novel last-iterate rate of order involving the variance at the solution, and a second last-iterate rate valid under arbitrary positive non-increasing stepsizes bounded by 1/(L n), generalizing prior results that needed a restrictive fixed stepsize.
conclusion: The shadow sequence technique relaxes stepsize requirements for RR analysis and may extend to other shuffling-based optimization methods.

title: Curvature-Scaled Sharpness-Aware Minimization: Convergence Beyond Smoothness
authors: Nicolas Loizou Dimitris Oikonomou
abstract: ArXiv:2610.29192v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) has established itself as a widely used method for training deep neural networks. Despite its popularity, existing convergence guarantees for SAM-type methods require smoothness, a restrictive assumption. Generalized smoothness conditions have recently been proposed in the analysis of gradient methods but remain underexplored for SAM. To analyze the effect of SAM's perturbation under generalized smoothness, we use relative gradient distortion to quantify how the sharpness-aware direction departs from the original gradient. Under [MATH]-smoothness, we show that this distortion can become unbounded near stationarity for SAM and at large gradients for its unnormalized variant (USAM), with examples where SAM cycles and USAM diverges. We then establish a necessary condition for uniform distortion control among perturbations along the gradient whose nonnegative multipliers depend only on its norm. Motivated by this condition, we propose Curvature-Scaled SAM (CS-SAM), which scales both the perturbation and the descent step by suitable curvature upper bounds, and prove that it uniformly bounds the distortion. Under both [MATH]- and [MATH]-smoothness, we establish deterministic [MATH] rates for the best squared gradient norm on nonconvex objectives, last-iterate [MATH] rates for the function gap on convex objectives with a minimizer, and linear convergence under the Polyak-Lojasiewicz condition. With zero perturbation, our guarantees recover the rates for gradient descent with [MATH]- or [MATH]-based step-sizes. Minibatch experiments on computer vision tasks demonstrate competitive performance for both variants, with the [MATH] variant achieving the highest mean best-test accuracy in all four settings against tuned SAM and USAM with constant and cosine annealing schedules.
tldr: The paper analyzes Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) under generalized smoothness assumptions and proposes Curvature-Scaled SAM (CS-SAM), which provably bounds gradient distortion and achieves standard convergence rates.
motivation: Existing convergence guarantees for SAM require restrictive smoothness assumptions; the behavior of SAM's perturbation under recently proposed generalized smoothness conditions is underexplored.
method: The authors quantify the departure of SAM's sharpness-aware direction from the gradient via relative gradient distortion, derive a necessary condition for uniform distortion control, and introduce CS-SAM, which scales both perturbation and descent step by curvature upper bounds.
result: Under L-smoothness-type conditions, CS-SAM yields deterministic O(1/sqrt(T)) rates for squared gradient norm in the nonconvex case, last-iterate rates on convex objectives, and linear convergence under the Polyak-Lojasiewicz condition; minibatch vision experiments show competitive accuracy.
conclusion: Curvature-scaled perturbations and steps restore provable convergence guarantees for SAM beyond standard smoothness, matching gradient descent rates in the zero-perturbation limit.

title: On The Existence Of Independent Inner Functions
authors: Xiangdi Fu, Kunyu Guo, Dilong Li, Yanqi Qiu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.29198v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The existence of independent inner functions is established: there exist inner functions [MATH] and [MATH], both vanishing at the origin, such that $[MATH][MATH]\varphi[MATH]\psi$ can be chosen to be Blaschke products. The proof proceeds by an iterative construction, which suggests a general approach to produce inner functions with a desired joint distribution.
tldr: The authors prove the existence of independent inner functions whose product can be made to be Blaschke products, using an iterative construction.
motivation: Inner functions and Blaschke products are central objects in Hardy space theory and operator theory, and understanding when independent inner functions exist relates to joint distribution problems in function theory.
method: An iterative construction is used to build two inner functions vanishing at the origin such that a product involving them is a Blaschke product.
result: Such independent inner functions are shown to exist, and the construction suggests a general scheme for producing inner functions with a prescribed joint distribution.
conclusion: The work establishes a new existence result in complex function theory and hints at broader constructions, but has no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: A Hybridization-derived Interior Penalty Nitsche Method For Heterogeneous And Anisotropic Diffusion
authors: Vincent Fontaine
abstract: ArXiv:2610.29214v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop an interior penalty Nitsche finite element formulation for heterogeneous and anisotropic diffusion problems, which is derived from an interior-penalty stabilized Lagrange multiplier method.
