A distinctive feature of the derived method is that it simultaneously combines two popular stabilization strategies: (i) a boundary penalty mechanism similar to Nitsche's methods and (ii) an interior penalty mechanism as for Continuous Interior Penalty (CIP) methods. Furthermore, the normal component of the numerical flux is single-valued across the mesh skeleton and available in closed form. We establish the equivalence between the hybridized Lagrange multiplier formulation and its condensed Interior Penalty Nitsche (IPN) form, and we deliver the stability and convergence analysis of the latter. For sufficiently regular solutions, we establish energy-norm error estimates for the three symmetry variants. Under a piecewise elliptic regularity assumption on the adjoint problem, the [MATH] estimate is optimal for the symmetric variant and exhibits a half-order loss for the incomplete and nonsymmetric variants; its constant may depend on the diffusion coefficients through the adjoint regularity constant. This single-valued numerical normal flux, available in closed form, provides a starting point for locally conservative [MATH]-conforming flux reconstruction, left for future work. Numerical experiments validate the theoretical findings.
tldr: The paper introduces an Interior Penalty Nitsche (IPN) finite element method for heterogeneous and anisotropic diffusion problems, derived from an interior-penalty stabilized Lagrange multiplier formulation.
motivation: Heterogeneous and anisotropic diffusion problems require robust numerical schemes, and the authors aim to combine boundary Nitsche-type penalties with continuous interior penalty stabilization to obtain a single-valued, closed-form numerical normal flux.
method: The authors derive the IPN formulation by hybridization from a stabilized Lagrange multiplier method, prove equivalence between the hybridized and condensed forms, and carry out stability and convergence analysis including energy-norm error estimates for three symmetry variants.
result: Energy-norm error estimates are established for sufficiently regular solutions, with optimal L2 estimates for the symmetric variant and a half-order loss for incomplete and nonsymmetric variants under piecewise elliptic regularity, supported by numerical experiments.
conclusion: The proposed IPN method provides a single-valued numerical normal flux suitable as a starting point for locally conservative flux reconstruction, with theoretical guarantees validated numerically.

title: Local Lyapunov Exponent-Guided Stochastic Midcourse Correction Design Of Low-Energy Earth-Moon Transfers
authors: Zihang Wang, Shuyue Fu, Di Wu, Shengping Gong
abstract: ArXiv:2610.29390v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Midcourse correction is essential for reliable cislunar transfer missions. For low-energy Earth-Moon transfers, strongly nonuniform error growth makes conventional correction strategies less effective. This paper proposes a stochastic midcourse correction design for low-energy Earth-Moon transfers based on local Lyapunov exponent (LLE). The local error-amplification characteristics of the nominal trajectory are first analyzed using an instantaneous LLE. The analysis shows that strong sensitivity is concentrated near periapsis, and that the LLE maxima coincide with regions of strong finite-time error growth. These maxima are therefore used to segment the trajectory and define the number of corrections. Based on this segmentation, a reduced parameterization is introduced to describe the correction epochs, while second-order state transition tensors (STTs) are employed for nonlinear correction targeting. The resulting timing variables are then optimized through a sample-average approximation of the chance-constrained stochastic problem. Paired Monte Carlo simulations show that, under the same mission-accuracy requirements, the proposed strategy greatly improves the reliability and robustness of trajectory recovery while requiring less correction cost than the classical Breakwell spacing-ratio strategy.
tldr: The paper proposes a stochastic midcourse correction strategy for low-energy Earth-Moon transfers that uses local Lyapunov exponents to segment the trajectory and optimize correction epochs under chance constraints.
motivation: Strongly nonuniform error growth in low-energy cislunar transfers makes conventional midcourse correction strategies ineffective, motivating a trajectory-specific, sensitivity-guided correction design.
method: Instantaneous local Lyapunov exponents are computed along the nominal trajectory to identify high-sensitivity regions near periapsis and define correction epochs; second-order state transition tensors provide nonlinear targeting, and timing variables are optimized via sample-average approximation of a chance-constrained stochastic problem.
result: Paired Monte Carlo simulations show the strategy substantially improves reliability and robustness of trajectory recovery while requiring lower correction cost than the classical Breakwell spacing-ratio strategy under identical accuracy requirements.
conclusion: Lyapunov-exponent-guided segmentation offers an efficient and robust framework for stochastic midcourse correction in highly sensitive low-energy lunar transfer design.

title: A High-order Multi-scale Method And Its Error Analysis For Nonlocal-in-time Fractionally Damped Wave Problems In Composite Materials
authors: Gehao Wang, Hao Dong, Yufeng Nie, Junzhi Cui
abstract: ArXiv:2610.29451v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Significant spatial heterogeneity and nonlocal history-dependent attenuation jointly govern wave propagation in composite materials, making full-scale direct numerical simulation (DNS) computationally prohibitive. This study proposed a high-order multi-scale (HOMS) method for nonlocal-in-time fractionally damped wave problems with highly oscillatory and discontinuous material coefficients. Using a multi-scale asymptotic expansion approach, the macroscopic homogenized equation, and first- and second-order correction terms are derived to construct the high-accuracy HOMS solution. Moreover, a local pointwise error analysis identifies the leading residual eliminated by this HOMS solution and validates its local physical balance preservation. Then, a global energy-norm error estimate establishes the [MATH]-order convergence rate for the HOMS solution. Subsequently, an efficient spatiotemporal multi-scale algorithm integrating the finite element and finite difference methods is designed, which employs a novel fully discrete [MATH]-Newmark scheme, and corresponding unconditional shifted-energy stability and explicit convergence rates are also obtained for the macroscopic homogenized displacement and velocity, respectively. Both two- and three-dimensional examples are presented to demonstrate the accuracy, efficiency, reduced cost, and robustness of the proposed HOMS method. This work provides an effective multi-scale tool for nonlocal-in-time wave simulation in engineering applications.
tldr: The paper develops a high-order multi-scale numerical method with error analysis for nonlocal-in-time fractionally damped wave propagation in heterogeneous composite materials.
motivation: Full-scale direct numerical simulation of wave propagation in composite materials is computationally prohibitive because of spatial heterogeneity and nonlocal history-dependent attenuation.
method: A multi-scale asymptotic expansion derives a homogenized macroscopic equation with first- and second-order corrections, and a fully discrete Newmark-type finite element/finite difference scheme is proposed.
result: Local pointwise error analysis and global energy-norm estimates establish convergence rates, while numerical examples in two and three dimensions demonstrate accuracy, efficiency, and robustness.
conclusion: The proposed high-order multi-scale framework provides an effective computational tool for engineering simulations of nonlocal-in-time wave problems in composite materials.

title: Black-Box Red-Teaming Of Multi-Agent Systems Via Reinforcement Learning
authors: Yuqi Jia, Hangsheng Zhang, Chenxi Liu, Junjie Liang, Xun Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2610.28966v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed in multi-agent systems (MAS) to accomplish complex tasks. Prior black-box red-teaming attacks mainly focus on single agents, but we find that these methods are far less effective in MAS, where multiple sub-agents may not directly interact with the user. Therefore, we introduce ReMAS, the first reinforcement learning-based red-teaming framework tailored to MASs, which fine-tunes attacker LLMs to generate effective adversarial prompts for system prompt extraction. The framework follows a two-step process: first, a rewrite stage refines base attack prompts to increase extraction success, and second, a template generation stage constructs attack templates that improve the likelihood of invoking specific sub-agents and thus revealing their system prompts. Extensive experiments show that our method substantially improves attack success rates compared to existing black-box attacks, with transferability across different backend LLMs and MAS structures. These results underscore the vulnerabilities of multi-agent systems and the importance of developing stronger defenses against adaptive black-box adversaries.
tldr: ReMAS is a reinforcement-learning-based black-box red-teaming framework that fine-tunes attacker LLMs to extract system prompts from multi-agent LLM systems.
motivation: Existing black-box red-teaming attacks are designed for single LLM agents and prove far less effective against multi-agent systems, where sub-agents may not interact directly with the user, leaving MAS vulnerabilities underexplored.
method: The framework uses a two-stage process: a rewrite stage that refines base attack prompts to boost extraction success, followed by a template generation stage that builds attack templates increasing the likelihood of invoking specific sub-agents and exposing their system prompts, with attacker LLMs trained via reinforcement learning.
result: Experiments show substantially higher attack success rates than existing black-box baselines, with transferability across different backend LLMs and MAS structures.
conclusion: Multi-agent LLM systems are notably vulnerable to adaptive black-box adversaries, motivating stronger defenses and further red-teaming research.

title: Beyond Tokens: NumAnchor For Address-Grounded Numeric Operand Representation In Assembly Language Models
authors: Kun Liu, Keith Mitchell, Xin Hu, Jiangcheng Yu, Chenke Luo, Zhengming Ding, Haotian Zhang, Jiang Ming
abstract: ArXiv:2610.29027v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Assembly language models (ALMs) are becoming important for automated binary analysis, yet their token-level interfaces often obscure numeric-like operands. In two corpora, such operands account for 45.7% and 40.9% of operand occurrences and may denote branch targets, global data, stack slots, constants, or unresolved pointer-derived values. Existing normalization strategies often lose their identities and structural relationships. We present NumAnchor, an input-boundary adapter that represents recoverable numeric-like operands as typed, canonicalized program entities. NumAnchor encodes code, data, and stack context in compact structural side descriptors, preserving entity identity and locality without increasing the host sequence length. These descriptors are fused into input embeddings before the first Transformer layer, while the host architecture, pretraining objectives, and downstream protocols remain unchanged. Probing frozen instruction-level embeddings yields 98.7% hierarchical-location accuracy and AUROC scores of 0.932 and 0.907 for jump and call target alignment, respectively, showing that the encoded structural information remains recoverable. Across multiple ALM families, NumAnchor achieves relative improvements of up to 35.0% in Recall@1 and 31.7% in MRR on 10k-candidate function retrieval, and improves execution-aware type recovery by up to 5.2 F1 points. Ablations show complementary gains from code, data, and stack descriptors with modest overhead.
tldr: NumAnchor is an input-boundary adapter that encodes numeric-like operands in assembly code as typed, canonicalized program entities fused into embeddings, improving assembly language model performance on retrieval and type recovery tasks.
motivation: Token-level interfaces of assembly language models obscure numeric-like operands (roughly 40-46% of operand occurrences) that carry branch-target, data, stack, and pointer semantics, and existing normalization discards their identity and structure.
method: The authors represent recoverable numeric-like operands as canonicalized typed entities, encode code/data/stack context in compact structural side descriptors, and fuse these descriptors into input embeddings before the first Transformer layer without changing the host architecture or training objectives.
result: Probing frozen embeddings yields 98.7% hierarchical-location accuracy and AUROC of 0.932/0.907 for jump/call target alignment, while end-to-end gains reach up to 35.0% relative Recall@1 and 31.7% MRR on 10k-candidate function retrieval plus up to 5.2 F1 points on execution-aware type recovery.
conclusion: Structured, identity-preserving operand representations can be injected cheaply at the input boundary to substantially improve binary-analysis performance of assembly language models.

title: Post-Pruning Vs. Early Stopping: Which Works Better For Link Prediction With AnyBurl?
authors: Thomas Eiter, Davide Sold\`a, Hai Xia
abstract: ArXiv:2610.29287v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Rule-based link prediction combines symbolic and statistical artificial intelligence methods by inductively learning a set of rules from a knowledge graph (KG), with the aim of completing the graph when a query cannot be answered from the KG alone. Several systems have been proposed, and while they perform well on classical benchmarks, even compared with embedding-based systems, many of them produce a large number of rules. This compromises scalability in the query-answering phase, especially under strong hardware constraints. In this work, we investigate the behavior of AnyBurl, a state-of-the-art rule learner for link prediction, to determine whether running it for a given time and then pruning the learned rules yields better query-answering performance at test time than a simpler approach that stops rule generation earlier.
tldr: The paper compares post-pruning of learned rules against early stopping of rule generation in AnyBurl, a rule-based link prediction system for knowledge graphs.
motivation: Rule learners for link prediction often generate very large rule sets, which hurts scalability at query-answering time, particularly under tight hardware constraints.
method: Empirical investigation of AnyBurl's behavior: running rule learning for a fixed time followed by pruning is compared with stopping rule generation earlier, evaluated on query-answering performance at test time.
result: The study characterizes the trade-off between post-hoc pruning and early stopping in terms of predictive performance and rule-set size at test time.
conclusion: The findings provide practical guidance on configuring AnyBurl for link prediction under resource constraints.

title: Gsp Autobidding Equilibria With Few Advertisers Or Slots
authors: Yiyang Huang, Zhengyang Liu, Yonglei Yan, Zihe Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.29310v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In sponsored-shopping auctions, one advertiser may win several positions, and a product that is never displayed may determine the prices of several winners. Under generalized second-price (GSP) pricing without self-pricing, these interactions couple allocation and payment through a single global ranking. We prove that exact autobidding equilibria under budget and return-on-investment (ROI) constraints can be computed in polynomial time whenever either the number [MATH] of advertisers or the number [MATH] of display slots is fixed. Our algorithms rely on two structural reductions. With few advertisers, the payment polytopes of tied bid layers combine by a Minkowski sum, giving a fixed-dimensional representation of exponentially many rankings. With few slots, budget equilibria admit threshold recovery and an exact submodular description of attainable payments at the display boundary. For ROI, we prove that every group-consecutive equilibrium has a representative with at most [MATH] nonunit multipliers, preserving the item and price in every displayed slot. In each case, the reduction leads to polynomially many systems of polynomial equations and inequalities in bounded dimension. The algorithms compute exact multipliers and explicit distributions over valid group-consecutive rankings, with support at most [MATH]; for ROI with few slots, this improves to [MATH].
tldr: The paper proves that exact autobidding equilibria in generalized second-price (GSP) sponsored-search auctions with budget and ROI constraints are computable in polynomial time when either the number of advertisers or the number of slots is fixed.
motivation: Sponsored-shopping auctions couple allocation and payment through a single global ranking, since one advertiser can occupy several positions and undisplayed products can set prices; computing equilibrium outcomes under autobidding constraints is therefore algorithmically challenging.
method: Two structural reductions are developed: with few advertisers, payment polytopes of tied bid layers combine via Minkowski sums to give a fixed-dimensional representation of exponentially many rankings; with few slots, budget equilibria admit threshold recovery and an exact submodular description of attainable payments, and ROI equilibria are shown to have representatives with few nonunit multipliers.
result: Each case reduces to polynomially many systems of polynomial equations and inequalities in bounded dimension, yielding exact multipliers and explicit distributions over group-consecutive rankings with bounded support size.
conclusion: Exact autobidding equilibria in GSP auctions are tractable in the parameterized sense of few advertisers or few slots, with improved support bounds for ROI equilibria with few slots.

title: Masar: Multi-stage Attack Surface Analysis And Reasoning Framework For Telecom Networks
authors: Heba Osama, Wessam Deifallah, Ahmed Saafan, Haitham Ghalwash
abstract: ArXiv:2610.29343v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The increasing complexity of modern telecommunications networks introduces security challenges that require systematic threat analysis. However, a gap remains between architectural threat modeling frameworks, such as Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information Disclosure, Denial of Service, and Elevation of Privilege (STRIDE), and operational knowledge bases, such as the MITRE Five-G Hierarchy of Threats (FiGHT). This gap limits the ability to connect architectural weaknesses with specific protocol behaviors and attack sequences. This paper presents Multi-stage Attack Surface Analysis and Reasoning (MASAR), a formal framework that bridges this gap through three layers: strategic threat mapping, logical attack path decomposition using directed acyclic graphs (DAGs), and operational synthesis of tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs). MASAR is evaluated using a 5G-ready IP Multimedia Subsystem (IMS) architecture, examining two signaling attack scenarios: early media billing bypass through Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) signaling and subscriber information disclosure and topology discovery through the Diameter Cx interface. MiniZinc constraint models are used to analyze the reachability of unsafe protocol states. The analysis demonstrates how MASAR connects architectural threats with specific protocol behaviors and supports security controls that account for network states in telecommunications systems.
tldr: MASAR is a three-layer formal framework that bridges architectural threat modeling (STRIDE) and operational threat knowledge bases (MITRE FiGHT) for telecom networks, demonstrated on two 5G IMS signaling attack scenarios.
motivation: Modern telecom networks are increasingly complex, and a gap exists between high-level architectural threat models and the concrete protocol-level attack behaviors catalogued in operational knowledge bases, limiting systematic security reasoning.
method: The framework combines strategic threat mapping, logical attack-path decomposition via directed acyclic graphs, and operational synthesis of TTPs; MiniZinc constraint models are used to check reachability of unsafe protocol states in a 5G-ready IMS architecture (SIP early-media billing bypass and Diameter Cx information disclosure).
result: MASAR successfully links architectural threats to specific protocol behaviors and attack sequences, enabling state-aware security controls in the two analyzed signaling attack scenarios.
conclusion: The framework provides a structured bridge between threat modeling and operational attack intelligence for telecom security, though it is a classical cybersecurity contribution with no quantum information, thermodynamics, network quantum, or hybrid-system component.

title: CertMoE: Robustness Certification For Mixture-of-Experts LLMs Via Routing-Aware Smoothing
authors: Qingyue Wang, Yudong Gao, Lixia Wang, Ruixuan Huang, Yuanyuan Yuan, Yangqiu Song, Shuai Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.29395v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Provable robustness is a cornerstone of trustworthy machine learning, aiming to guarantee model predictions under adversarial perturbations. Existing certification frameworks, inspired by abstract interpretation or symbolic execution, typically assume a fixed computation graph, where input perturbations or variations affect only model outputs but not the underlying execution path. This assumption, however, is violated in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) Large Language Models (LLMs), whose input-dependent routing induces discrete and dynamic execution paths. Crucially, this dynamic computation changes the certified object from a single fixed function to a composition of input-dependent sub-functions, leading to unreliable certification guarantees. This paper presents , the first routing-aware robustness certification framework for MoE LLMs, which explicitly accounts for input-induced routing dynamics in certification. Specifically, we introduce a relaxed routing-containment criterion, which certifies that perturbed Top-[MATH] routing is contained within a larger certified expert pool. Based on this guarantee, then constructs the corresponding induced sub-network and certifies its prediction consistency. This hierarchical certification procedure yields a joint probabilistic guarantee over routing containment and sub-network robustness, providing sufficient conditions under which the original prediction remains invariant. Extensive experiments across recent MoE LLMs demonstrate that dynamic routing makes certificates issued by existing methods frequently violated, while reduces the empirical violation rate with routing-aware guarantees, e.g., from more than [MATH] to [MATH], yielding certificates that more faithfully reflect the robustness of MoE models.
tldr: The paper introduces CertMoE, the first routing-aware robustness certification framework for Mixture-of-Experts LLMs that accounts for input-dependent discrete routing dynamics.
motivation: Existing provable-robustness certification frameworks assume a fixed computation graph, an assumption violated by MoE LLMs whose data-dependent Top-k routing changes the executed sub-network and thus invalidates standard certificates.
method: CertMoE introduces a relaxed routing-containment criterion certifying that perturbed Top-k routing stays inside a larger certified expert pool, then builds the induced sub-network and certifies its prediction consistency, yielding a joint probabilistic guarantee.
result: Experiments on recent MoE LLMs show existing certificates are frequently violated under dynamic routing, whereas routing-aware certificates sharply reduce empirical violation rates (e.g., from above 30% to under 1%).
conclusion: Explicitly modeling routing dynamics is necessary for trustworthy certification of MoE models and yields certificates that more faithfully reflect their true robustness.

title: VMSpec: A Decompiler-based Approach Against Virtual Machine Obfuscation
authors: Fabian Kilger, Leonard Auer, Manuel Andreas
abstract: ArXiv:2610.29566v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Malicious actors frequently obfuscate their code to hinder investigative reverse engineering efforts. Among the most formidable techniques is virtual machine (VM) obfuscation: programs are translated into bytecode for a custom VM, often with a randomized virtual instruction set and distributed alongside a corresponding interpreter. Manual analysis and deobfuscation scale poorly due to the complexity of VM obfuscation and the diversification techniques that render each VM and interpreter unique. Existing methods primarily focus on simplifying execution traces and identifying virtual execution boundaries. However, comparatively little attention has been given to recovering higher-level program semantics from VM-obfuscated code. To address this gap, we propose VMSpec, a novel decompiler-based approach that automates the construction of VM processor specifications, enabling existing, well-known decompilers to analyze the VM-obfuscated code. We evaluate our prototype of VMSpec on 147 programs from an established obfuscation benchmark, comprising hash functions, standard algorithms, and randomized functions, obfuscated with different configurations of the Tigress and Code Virtualizer obfuscators. To demonstrate real-world applicability, we additionally include six domain generation algorithms stemming from real-world malware. VMSpec completely strips VM-obfuscation from nearly all obfuscated samples, producing output comparable to Ghidra's decompilation of the original code. Furthermore, it is the first method capable of reconstructing the complete program behavior of VM-obfuscated programs with infinite, input-dependent paths and recursive calls.
tldr: VMSpec is a decompiler-based tool that automatically reconstructs virtual machine processor specifications so off-the-shelf decompilers can strip VM obfuscation from malware binaries.
motivation: VM obfuscation, in which code is compiled to a randomized custom bytecode with a bundled interpreter, defeats manual reverse engineering and scales poorly for analysts; existing work focuses on trace simplification and boundary detection rather than recovering high-level semantics.
method: The authors build a prototype that automatically derives VM processor specifications from obfuscated binaries and feeds them to existing decompilers, and they evaluate it on 147 benchmark programs obfuscated with Tigress and Code Virtualizer plus six real-world malware domain generation algorithms.
result: VMSpec removes VM obfuscation from nearly all samples, yielding decompiled output comparable to Ghidra's decompilation of the unobfuscated originals, and is the first method to recover full program behavior for samples with infinite, input-dependent paths and recursion.
conclusion: Automated recovery of VM semantics via processor-spec construction makes general-purpose decompilers effective against VM obfuscation, offering a practical advance for malware analysis.

title: S-pass: Star-Topology Pinching-Antenna Systems With Pipelined Antenna Pre-Positioning
authors: Hans D. Schotten Wei Jiang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.29700v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Pinching-antenna systems (PASS) flexibly reconfigure the wireless channel by positioning dielectric antennas along a waveguide near each user. Releasing and re-attaching an antenna, however, is a mechanical operation orders of magnitude slower than electronic switching, wasting much transmission time. Existing designs generally assume instant reconfiguration, neglect the mechanical latency, or keep the antenna fixed. This paper proposes S-PASS, a star architecture of waveguides sharing one radio-frequency chain through a switch, and pipelined antenna pre-positioning (PAP), a time-division protocol in which idle waveguides pre-position their antennas for their next users while one transmits. It derives in closed form the scheduling efficiency, the number of waveguides beyond which the latency costs no transmission time, and the latency up to which PAP outperforms fixed placement. Analytical and numerical results show that this latency grows with each added waveguide, and users at the outer ends of the waveguides gain most.
tldr: S-PASS proposes a star-topology pinching-antenna system with a pipelined antenna pre-positioning protocol that hides mechanical antenna re-attachment latency behind transmission time.
motivation: Releasing and re-attaching pinching dielectric antennas along a waveguide is mechanically slow compared with electronic switching, so existing PASS designs that assume instant reconfiguration waste substantial transmission time.
method: The authors introduce a star architecture of waveguides sharing one RF chain through a switch, plus a time-division protocol in which idle waveguides pre-position their antennas for future users while one waveguide transmits; they derive closed-form scheduling efficiency, the waveguide count beyond which latency is fully hidden, and the latency threshold at which pre-positioning beats fixed placement.
result: Closed-form and numerical analyses show the tolerable latency grows with each added waveguide, and users located at the outer waveguide ends benefit most from pipelined pre-positioning.
conclusion: Pipelined antenna pre-positioning makes mechanically reconfigured PASS practical for multi-user access by amortizing antenna repositioning latency across parallel waveguides.

title: The Geometry Of Wigwag And Reversal Linework In Blown Glass
authors: Anduriel Widmark
abstract: ArXiv:2610.28668v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Wigwag and reversal linework in blown glass produces periodic wave, spiral, and radiating patterns by twisting longitudinal stripes in alternating directions and then reorganizing the patterned tube. Although glassworkers have developed many consistent techniques and identifiable pattern forms, these patterns do not appear to have been widely described within a common coordinate framework. This paper presents one way of modeling these patterns mathematically. Periodic linework is defined on a cylinder, represented on a sphere, and read relative to a switched axis. The switched pattern may then be re-formed into cylindrical or circular configurations and further manipulated into square, rectangular, or compound forms. The circular case provides a particularly simple radial representation of the switched spherical field. This sequence describes the characteristic organization of a reversal, with the same geometry extending to stacked encalmo sections and other compound structures. The goal is to provide a concise mathematical language for interpreting this broad family of patterned glass forms.
tldr: The paper proposes a mathematical coordinate framework for describing periodic wigwag and reversal linework patterns in blown glass.
motivation: Glassworkers have developed consistent techniques and recognizable pattern forms, but these lack a shared mathematical description, making cross-comparison and teaching difficult.
method: Patterns are modeled as periodic linework on a cylinder, mapped onto a sphere, read relative to a switched axis, and then re-formed into cylindrical, circular, square, rectangular, or compound configurations.
result: The circular case yields a simple radial representation of the switched spherical field, and the same geometric sequence extends to stacked encalmo sections and other compound structures.
conclusion: The framework offers a concise mathematical language for interpreting a broad family of patterned glass forms, aiding description and pedagogy in glassmaking.

title: Deflation-Based Spectral Preconditioning For The Conjugate Gradient Method On Perturbed Systems
authors: Youssef Diouane, Selime G\"urol, Oussama Mouhtal, Dominique Orban
abstract: ArXiv:2610.28808v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider sequences of large symmetric positive-definite linear systems in which spectral information from a reference matrix [MATH] is reused to accelerate the solution of a nearby system with perturbed matrix [MATH], where [MATH] is symmetric, [MATH], and [MATH] is the perturbation size. We compare deflated conjugate gradient (deflated CG) with preconditioned CG (PCG) equipped with a scaled spectral preconditioner constructed from the same spectral information of [MATH]. First, we derive an energy-norm error characterization of deflated CG. We then use perturbation analysis to show that, after one additional PCG iteration, the squared PCG error is bounded, up to terms of order [MATH], by an explicit multiple of the squared deflated CG error. This result clarifies the role of the scaling parameter in the preconditioner. Experiments show that the scaled spectral preconditioner recovers much of the convergence improvement provided by deflation while requiring fewer products with [MATH].
tldr: The paper compares deflated conjugate gradient with a scaled spectral preconditioner for solving sequences of perturbed symmetric positive-definite linear systems.
motivation: It aims to reuse spectral information from a reference matrix to accelerate convergence for nearby perturbed systems and to clarify the role of the preconditioner scaling parameter.
method: The authors derive an energy-norm error characterization for deflated CG and perform perturbation analysis bounding the squared PCG error in terms of the squared deflated CG error after one additional iteration.
result: The analysis shows that the scaled spectral preconditioner can recover much of the convergence improvement of deflation while requiring fewer products with the reference matrix.
conclusion: The proposed preconditioning approach offers a practical alternative to deflation for perturbed linear systems, supported by theoretical bounds and numerical experiments.

title: Mixed Finite Element Methods For A Heat-assisted Model Of Sedimentation
authors: Cristian Inzunza Julio Careaga
abstract: ArXiv:2610.28903v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A model for the consolidation-sedimentation process incorporating thermal effects is analysed. The model is motivated by novel applications to heat-assisted sedimentation of mineral suspensions. A system of convection-diffusion equations for the concentration and temperature are coupled to flow equations for the volume-average velocity and pressure. The model is supplemented with Dirichlet and mixed boundary conditions. A quasi-stationary approach of the system is analysed by means of a mixed variational formulation, where additional variables such as the pseudostress tensor and variables for the gradient of the temperature and concentration are introduced. The existence and uniqueness of the system is shown making use of the Babu{\v s}ka-Brezzi theory and Banach's fixed-point theorem, under hypotheses of smallness of the data and additional regularity on the solutions. A discrete formulation based on finite element spaces is proposed and analysed, and the existence of solutions is achieved thanks to Brouwer's fixed-point theorem. Additionally, C\'ea and a priori estimates are derived for the mixed formulation. Finally, numerical examples are provided to demonstrate the performance of the model and to confirm the theoretical rates of convergence.
tldr: The paper develops and analyzes mixed finite element methods for a heat-assisted sedimentation model coupling concentration, temperature, velocity, and pressure.
motivation: The work is motivated by heat-assisted sedimentation of mineral suspensions and aims to provide a rigorous numerical framework for the coupled consolidation-sedimentation process with thermal effects.
method: The authors use a mixed variational formulation introducing pseudostress and gradient variables, prove well-posedness via Babuška-Brezzi theory and Banach's fixed-point theorem, and propose a finite element discretization analyzed with Brouwer's fixed-point theorem and Céa/a priori estimates.
result: Existence and uniqueness are established under small-data and regularity assumptions, convergence rates are derived, and numerical examples confirm the theoretical rates.
conclusion: The paper provides a mathematically rigorous mixed finite element approach for heat-assisted sedimentation, but it is unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: A Link-Based Algorithm For Stochastic User Equilibrium With Bounded Choice And Local Detour Threshold
authors: Takeshi Nagae
abstract: ArXiv:2610.29151v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This study develops a novel solution method for stochastic user equilibrium (SUE) under the bounded choice model with local detour threshold (BCM-LDT SUE; Rasmussen et al., 2024), which restricts the choice set in line with observed route choice behavior. The model assigns zero probability to paths whose total cost exceeds a bound or whose local detour exceeds a threshold; thus, the path choice set varies with link costs. The proposed algorithm updates link flows while implicitly enumerating the path choice set via a depth-first search (DFS) pruned with the BCM-LDT bounds. This distinguishes it from the original algorithm, which updates path flows, and enables quasi-Newton-type acceleration. Since paths are never stored, the method can handle choice sets totaling on the order of [MATH] paths. On a personal computer, it reached equilibrium in a few to about fifteen minutes, not only for the Anaheim network under the original settings but also for larger networks such as Winnipeg and Barcelona.
tldr: The paper proposes a link-flow-based algorithm with depth-first-search path enumeration for solving stochastic user equilibrium under a bounded choice model with a local detour threshold.
motivation: Existing BCM-LDT SUE algorithms update path flows and require storing paths, which becomes impractical when choice sets are combinatorially large; a more scalable solution method is needed for realistic networks.
method: The authors update link flows while implicitly enumerating the path choice set via a depth-first search pruned by the BCM-LDT cost bound and local detour thresholds, which never stores paths and permits quasi-Newton-type acceleration.
result: On a personal computer the algorithm converged to equilibrium in a few to about fifteen minutes for the Anaheim network as well as larger networks such as Winnipeg and Barcelona, handling choice sets of enormous size.
conclusion: The link-based approach makes bounded-choice SUE tractable for large-scale networks without explicit path storage, offering a practical computational advance for traffic assignment.

title: Point Cloud Transmission With Patch-Based Rate Adaptation
authors: Shipeng Liu, Garima Bazard, Khac-Hoang Ngo, Per-Erik Forss\'en
abstract: ArXiv:2610.29479v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a joint source-channel coding (JSCC) framework for efficient wireless point cloud transmission. In the proposed scheme, the point cloud is first divided into local patches and transformed into compact latent representations, which are then mapped to symbols for transmission over a noisy channel. Our model incorporates an entropy model that exploits inter-patch spatial dependencies to estimate patch-level coding costs and allocate different numbers of symbols accordingly. Unlike existing patch-based point cloud JSCC methods that use the same transmission rate between patches, we adapt the channel usage of each patch latent representation. To exploit inter-patch dependencies without patch-by-patch autoregressive processing, we select a group of anchor patches whose features provide contextual information for entropy estimation of non-anchor ones. The framework is trained using a reconstruction loss and an entropy-based rate surrogate. Experiments on ModelNet40 demonstrate overall rate-distortion improvements over existing baselines across channel conditions.
tldr: A joint source-channel coding framework for wireless point cloud transmission that adapts per-patch symbol allocation using entropy models over inter-patch dependencies.
motivation: Point cloud data is large and must be transmitted efficiently over noisy wireless channels, and existing patch-based JSCC methods use uniform rates across patches, ignoring varying information content.
method: The point cloud is split into local patches, encoded into latent representations, and an entropy model with anchor patches provides context to estimate patch-level coding costs, which determine the number of channel symbols allocated to each patch; training uses reconstruction loss plus an entropy-based rate surrogate.
result: Experiments on ModelNet40 show rate-distortion improvements over existing baselines across a range of channel conditions.
conclusion: Patch-level rate adaptation with anchor-based context modeling yields more efficient point cloud JSCC than uniform-rate patch schemes.

title: Sign Here: Attributing A Source For A More Trustworthy Software Supply Chain
authors: Derek Garcia
abstract: ArXiv:2610.28794v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Software supply chain attacks continue to be on the rise, exploiting the trust that helps open source ecosystems thrive. Recent incidents like the Shai-Hulud worm and the Axios compromise demonstrate that a single malicious package can have wide reaching and devastating impacts overnight. These high profile attacks can be traced back to the same culprit: package registries. Although they are a useful convenience to pull prebuilt packages from, is such a commonly exploited component of the software supply chain worth the risk? In this paper, we investigate whether removing the registry from the developer workflow by building packages directly from source can serve as a malware prevention strategy - effectively removing an entire attack surface. Our hypothesis is that malicious packages avoid attributing a source to minimize visibility, while benign packages seek exposure and therefore link to their repositories. We evaluate this through three research questions: how effective is building from source at avoiding malware, how feasible is it to build from source in the current state of the supply chain, and how the building from source strategy compares to state-of-the-art security scanners. To do so, we (1) construct an aggregate dataset of 47,066 malicious packages from four academic and one industry malicious datasets source across npm and PyPI ecosystems, (2) build a snapshot index of all 3.9 million npm and 764 thousand PyPI packages, and (3) analyze all malicious samples alongside a statistically significant sample of 16,569 packages from each registry, totaling 33,138 packages. We find that simply checking for a source has a success rate between 87.7 and 99.9 percent of preventing malware, depending on the level of source vetting. Consequently, there is a significant lack of transparency within benign packages, with only 47.4 percent attributing a source an end user could build from.
tldr: The paper proposes building software packages directly from source, instead of relying on package registries, as a malware prevention strategy in software supply chains.
motivation: Software supply chain attacks often exploit trusted package registries, and malicious packages tend to hide their source repositories while benign packages usually link to them.
method: The authors assemble 47,066 malicious packages across npm and PyPI, index 3.9 million npm and 764 thousand PyPI packages, and analyze malicious samples plus a statistically significant benign sample for source-attribution and buildability.
result: Checking for a source repository prevents malware in 87.7–99.9% of cases depending on vetting level, but only 47.4% of benign packages attribute a source that an end user could build from.
conclusion: Removing package registries from the developer workflow by building from source can reduce attack surface, although current supply-chain transparency remains insufficient.

title: How Much Does The Harness Matter, And For Whom? A Multi-Model Study Of Context In LLM-Driven Vulnerability Discovery
authors: Ben Wilde Ganni Galea Curmi
abstract: ArXiv:2610.28802v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How much does an agent harness affect vulnerability discovery, and does its value depend on the model? We study 24 model-runner configurations using an open-source harness on a production codebase whose vulnerabilities were non-public at scan time. The pipeline combines static screening, LLM investigation, model self-revalidation, root-cause mapping, independent source review, and isolated proof-of-concept confirmation. Across 265 confirmed security root causes, the largest two-run configuration covers 60.4%, while 14.3% are found by exactly one model. No single configuration covers all observed findings. In a four-model context experiment, moving from a minimal prompt to an engineered prompt with a CodeQL-derived call graph raises criticality-weighted yield by 20-86% for smaller and mid-tier models, compared with 2% for the frontier model. This comparison changes both prompt and context. Separating those effects shows that the engineered prompt improves yield for all four models, while adding CodeQL context beyond that prompt improves yield only for the smallest model. A held-out CyberGym subset shows the same direction of target-recall improvement for the combined treatment. Frontier models achieve low false-report rates but do not consistently achieve the highest yield. Strong lower-cost models can deliver similar performance at an order of magnitude lower cost. These results support matching models, prompts, and context to the task, and combining configurations for broader coverage.
tldr: A multi-model empirical study of how agent harness design, prompt engineering, and CodeQL-derived context affect LLM-driven vulnerability discovery across 24 model-runner configurations.
motivation: Teams deploying LLM agents for security scanning need to know whether harness and context engineering matter, and whether their value varies by model size and cost.
method: The authors run 24 model-runner configurations on a production codebase with non-public vulnerabilities using an open-source pipeline combining static screening, LLM investigation, self-revalidation, root-cause mapping, independent review, and isolated PoC confirmation, plus a controlled four-model prompt/context ablation and a held-out CyberGym evaluation.
result: The best two-run configuration covers 60.4% of 265 confirmed root causes and 14.3% are found by exactly one model; engineered prompts raise criticality-weighted yield by 20-86% for small/mid-tier models versus 2% for the frontier model, with CodeQL context helping only the smallest model.
conclusion: Model, prompt, and context should be matched to the task, and combining heterogeneous configurations yields broader coverage; lower-cost strong models can approach frontier performance at far lower cost.

title: Beyond Policy Engines: Binding-Complete Execution Admission
authors: Lin Wang, Mengting Wu, Yong Zhang, Jiang Deng
abstract: ArXiv:2610.29701v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Policy engines determine whether evaluated policies permit a request, but a correct ALLOW decision does not establish complete governance-source participation, exact context binding, or sufficient grounds for execution admission. This paper examines the gap between policy evaluation and execution admission. We introduce the Binding-Complete Execution Admission Contract (BCEAC), a governance-relative contract for independently determined source obligations, exact policy and contextual binding, and typed admission outcomes under explicit trust assumptions. We propose a conditionally engine-agnostic architecture in which participating backends must satisfy declared semantic profiles, adapter contracts, and contextual correspondence obligations; an Execution Boundary Language (EBL) authoring syntax remains optional. The architecture separates governance resolution, policy evaluation, independent admission verification, and downstream execution mediation. We investigate two distinct experimental tracks: a finite Governance Source Completeness study and an OPA/Cedar experiment with archived native-engine records examined by offline review. The OPA/Cedar archive comprises 72 scenarios and 144 strict case-engine records (120 native-invoked and 24 pre-native), with eight additional permissive controls outside the strict denominator. The offline review did not rerun the original native OPA/Cedar executables. The results provide bounded evidence while retaining historical failures and unresolved implementation defects. The work does not establish constitutional adequacy, general semantic refinement, authenticated currentness, machine-checked execution-safety theorems, or protected external effects. Its contribution is an explicit, falsifiable framework for determining what must be established between a policy decision and an execution-admission judgment.
tldr: The paper proposes the Binding-Complete Execution Admission Contract (BCEAC), a governance framework specifying what must be verified between a policy ALLOW decision and actual execution admission.
motivation: Policy engines only decide whether a request is permitted, but an ALLOW outcome does not guarantee complete governance-source participation, exact context binding, or adequate grounds for execution, leaving a gap between policy evaluation and execution admission.
method: The authors introduce BCEAC, a governance-relative contract with typed admission outcomes and explicit trust assumptions, plus a conditionally engine-agnostic architecture separating governance resolution, policy evaluation, independent admission verification, and execution mediation; they run a Governance Source Completeness study and an offline review of archived OPA/Cedar records (72 scenarios, 144 case-engine records).
result: The offline review yields bounded evidence while retaining historical failures and unresolved defects, and explicitly does not rerun native OPA/Cedar executables; no machine-checked execution-safety theorems or authenticated currentness are established.
conclusion: The contribution is an explicit, falsifiable framework for determining what must be established between a policy decision and an execution-admission judgment, rather than a proof of constitutional adequacy or semantic refinement.

title: Optimal Dividends And Proactive Capital Injection Over A Finite Horizon
authors: Ran Xu, Zuo Quan Xu, Xueying Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.29085v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study a finite-horizon dividend and capital-injection problem for a Brownian surplus process with time-varying financing costs. Under a classical passive-injection policy, capital is supplied only at the solvency boundary. Anticipated increases in financing costs may instead make it optimal to inject capital while reserves remain strictly positive. We characterize this proactive financing mechanism through an auxiliary Dynkin game for the marginal value of liquidity. The game identifies an endogenous lower financing boundary and an upper dividend boundary, and yields restrictions on intervention timing and comparative statics with respect to the financing-cost path. Under a regular intervention-band condition, we recover the control value by spatial integration of the game value and verify that the optimal policy is two-sided reflection between the two boundaries. We establish this condition for a canonical class with decreasing marginal dividend rewards, increasing marginal financing costs, and a compatible piecewise affine terminal marginal value. Strictly decreasing financing costs eliminate positive-reserve financing contact and reduce the marginal game to a one-player stopping problem. Numerical examples illustrate the optimal policies and the effects of anticipated financing conditions on shareholder value and intervention thresholds.
tldr: The paper studies optimal dividend payments and proactive capital injection for a Brownian surplus process over a finite horizon with time-varying financing costs.
motivation: Anticipated increases in financing costs can make it optimal to inject capital before reserves reach the solvency boundary, motivating a finite-horizon control model with proactive financing.
method: The authors characterize the marginal value of liquidity via an auxiliary Dynkin game, identifying endogenous financing and dividend boundaries and recovering the control value under a regular intervention-band condition.
result: Under a canonical class with decreasing marginal dividend rewards and increasing marginal financing costs, the optimal policy is two-sided reflection between the financing and dividend boundaries, with comparative statics on financing-cost paths.
conclusion: The paper provides a theoretical framework for optimal dividend and proactive capital-injection policies, showing how anticipated financing conditions affect shareholder value and intervention thresholds.

title: PQ-Vault: Provably Quantum-Safe Asset Custody For Unmodified Ethereum
authors: Hassan Khodaiemehr, Khadijeh Bagheri, Chen Feng
abstract: ArXiv:2610.29230v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A quantum computer could recover the key of any Ethereum account whose public key appears on chain. We prove that no sidechain or bridge that leaves Ethereum's rules unchanged can protect such accounts: their funds must move into a contract whose release condition relies only on quantum-safe primitives. We design , a custody system for unmodified Ethereum combining this vault, a quantum-safe proof-of-stake sidechain whose checkpoints carry compact certificates, and an optimistic dispute protocol. We give the first security proof of compact certificates against quantum attackers and a matching attack: with classically chosen parameters, the guarantee falls from 128 to about 60 bits, and a simple rule restores it. We show that a common seed-update rule in hash-chain proof of stake lets an attacker steer chosen slots and profit from splitting its stake, and give an election whose steering gain and inclusion delay are provably bounded against quantum attackers. Since compressing certificates with a pairing-based SNARK breaks quantum security, we use fraud proofs that need a single signature check. For 65,536 validators, a certificate is 0.8 MB, 260 times smaller than all signatures, and verifies in about 20 ms; the vault accepts a checkpoint for about 420,000 gas.
tldr: Analysis failed
